Journal of Virology.title: Developing a fluorescent derivative of GagPol as a tool for live-cell imaging of HIV-1 assembly.
Journal of Virology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] The HIV-1 assembly process is driven by the structural polyprotein Gag, which forms small cytosolic oligomers that traffic to the plasma membrane. While Gag alone is sufficient to drive particle formation, the incorporation of GagPol, a polyprotein comprising Gag and viral enzymes, is essential for productive infection. Maintenance of the proper Gag:GagPol ratio is crucial for virion infectivity. Yet, the mechanisms regulating their cytosolic interactions remain incompletely understood, in part because most studies rely on ensemble biochemical assays that hide cell-to-cell heterogeneity and lack spatial and temporal resolution. To overcome these limitations and investigate the dynamics of GagPol at the molecular level, we systematically tested different approaches to fluorescently label it. We successfully produced two functional fluorescent GagPol variants: one single-labeled GagPol and a second double-labeled variant with a fluorescent protein added within Gag, which allows concurrent visualization of Gag and GagPol. These labeled versions, in combination with the use of raster image (cross-)correlation spectroscopy, enabled the quantification of Gag and GagPol relative concentrations and intermolecular interactions at the single-cell level. Overall, these variants set the stage for in-depth investigations of GagPol during HIV assembly, providing insights into cytoplasmic trafficking, particle assembly, and the kinetics of these processes. [IMPORTANCE] The participation of Gag and GagPol in HIV-1 assembly is central to the generation of infectious virions. While the structural role of Gag and the enzymatic functions of GagPol are well described, little is known regarding the mechanisms underlying their cytosolic interactions, spatial organization, and relative incorporation into assembling particles. Here, we successfully developed two stable fluorescently labeled variants of GagPol: a single-labeled variant with a label in the Pol domain and a double-labeled construct in which the Gag domain is also tagged. Using these constructs, we can quantitatively investigate Gag and GagPol interactions at the single-cell level. Hence, they provide a framework for a comprehensive study of the oligomerization properties and trafficking of these polyproteins at different stages of HIV-1 assembly, including membrane recruitment and incorporation into nascent virions.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: AlphaInterp: Revealing how AlphaFold 3 processes structure, confidence, and evolutionary information
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Jonathan Feldman, Jeffrey Skolnick How does evolutionary information become structural knowledge? AlphaFold 3 predicts protein structures and biomolecular assemblies with remarkable accuracy, yet how it transforms comparative sequence information into three-dimensional structure remains poorly understood. Here, we use mechanistic interpretability to follow this transformation through AlphaFold 3 and identify a computational principle underlying its structural inference. By extracting single- and pair-representations across the model’s forward pass and combining representational-geometry analysis, linear probing, activation patching, and perturbation of the multiple-sequence alignment (MSA) and its phylogenetic diversity, we show that AlphaFold 3 does not simply infer structure from raw sequence nor from MSA depth. Instead, a small number of sufficiently divergent homologues provides enough comparative information to largely recover the structure predicted using the full MSA. The pairformer transforms this evolutionary signal into a compact latent space in which residue-pair distances, contacts, fold similarity, and structural confidence become progressively decodable. Removing the MSA disrupts these latent geometries. Replacing it with evolutionarily similar homologues provides substantially less information, while evolutionarily unrelated sequences fail to rescue prediction despite preserving the formal alignment input. In contrast, phylogenetically diverse MSA subsampling largely restores both prediction accuracy and representational coherence. These results suggest that AlphaFold 3 has learned to infer structure by constraining its geometric priors and structural hypotheses by the sequence variation of the MSA. This framework helps explain both the model’s remarkable predictive power and its characteristic failure modes, with direct implications for protein design, conformational diversity, out-of-distribution generalization, and the interpretation of model confidence.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Gray bats heighten their response to social cues when navigating group flight in environments with obstacles
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Eighdi Aung, Nicole Abaid Bats are fast fliers with great maneuverability. Many species sense and communicate through echolocation, relying on acoustic signals in the environment. Bats also form large colonies, which necessitates that they fly in groups. When group size increases or obstacles are in their flight paths, the acoustic space can become cluttered, posing a non-trivial challenge for navigation. How do they interact with their environment and conspecifics, and how do they balance social and environmental cues? Recent research has uncovered individual adaptations to calling and flight patterns when flying in the groups or avoiding obstacles. Studies also suggest coordination when foraging, as well as strategies used by the group to mitigate acoustic clutter. However, there has yet to be a study on how bats weigh different navigational tasks when flying in spatially complex environments. Here, we collected stereoscopic video data from a wild colony of gray bats, Myotis grisescens, navigating their usual foraging flight paths in the presence of novel obstacles. We find that bats tend to stay close to a wall, but space out when flying in groups. We develop a data-informed agent-based model which reveals that their social repulsive behavior is strengthened when challenged to navigate novel obstacles.

Trends in Ecology & Evolution.title: Migration strategy and colonization: the disproportionate role of partial migration
authors: Paul Dufour, Alexander C. Lees, Jane M. Reid, Miriam Liedvogel, Santiago Claramunt, Pablo Capilla-Lasheras
Trends in Ecology & Evolution.abstract: Colonization drives diversification and determines how species shift their ranges, making it central to ecology and evolution. As both seasonal migration and dispersal depend on locomotor capacity, migration could be a major yet overlooked route to colonization. Here, we present evidence that partially migratory species are disproportionately successful in founding new populations, whereas strict migrants establish more rarely despite routinely reaching potentially suitable habitat in novel areas. Building on the threshold model of migration, we propose that partial migrants’ liability to migrate lies closer to the threshold and/or is more environmentally sensitive, allowing displaced individuals to settle. This mechanism can help explain species distributions and diversification and predict which species might colonize newly suitable areas under global environmental change.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Profiling of antibody responses to human norovirus in animals.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: Noroviruses are a major cause of acute gastroenteritis globally, with over 30 genotypes circulating in humans, some widespread, and others sporadically detected. Human noroviruses have been detected in a variety of animal species, raising the possibility that animals may serve as reservoirs or intermediate hosts for emerging human norovirus strains. To assess whether serology can reveal the circulation of human norovirus genotypes in animals, we analyzed antibody responses in 465 sera from 17 animal species using a previously established multiplex protein microarray containing P-particle antigens from 30 GI, GII, GIV, and GVI genotypes. High antibody titers to multiple antigens were observed in sera from cats, dogs, and several duck species, and chickens, whereas lower titers to fewer genotypes were observed in sera from rats, pigs, horses, and wild boar. Sera from macaques, sea lions, harbor porpoises, cattle, sheep, goats, and serotine bats showed low or undetectable antibody titers. Although we detected antibodies to common human genotypes in cats and dogs, antibodies in other animal species were primarily directed against sporadically reported genotypes. Ninety-five samples exhibited immunodominant responses, defined as one to three genotypes exhibiting higher antibody titers than the geometric mean of the remaining genotypes, and therefore suggestive of genotype-specific recognition. Binding-blocking assays performed on selected sera confirmed some antibody responses observed on the array. Although we find no clear evidence of human norovirus circulation in animals, the strong and broadly reactive antibody profiles observed in cats, dogs, and birds warrant further investigation.IMPORTANCEHuman noroviruses have been detected in multiple animal species, raising concerns that animals could act as reservoirs or intermediate hosts for emerging human norovirus strains. However, it remains unclear whether serological responses in animals reflect true circulation of human noroviruses or instead cross-reactive antibody recognition. Using a multiplex protein microarray spanning 30 norovirus genotypes, we profiled antibody responses in sera from 17 animal species. We detected broad antibody responses in cats, dogs, and several bird species, but found little evidence of consistent norovirus genotype-specific recognition. Binding-blocking assays confirmed some of the detected antibody responses. Together, our findings suggest that most antibody responses in animals likely reflect cross-reactivity or non-specific binding rather than widespread circulation of human noroviruses.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Effects of fine soils from former bauxite mines on phytopathogenic and biological control agent fungal strains.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Soil samples collected at 20 and 50 m around the entrances of three former bauxite mines in the Puglia region, Southern Italy, at San Giovanni Rotondo, Otranto, and Spinazzola, were characterized by pollutant total concentration (PTC), considering rare earth elements (REEs), toxic metals (TMs), and PTCREEs+TMs, Nemerow integrated risk index, and the modified contamination degree index. Samples were tested at 1% in potato dextrose agar (PDA) and as liquid cultures in half-strength potato dextrose broth (½PDB) against Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici (FOL), Sclerotinia minor (SM), Verticillium dahliae (VD), and Trichoderma harzianum (TH). Sampling locality and distance strongly influenced the biological effects of soil samples on fungal strains. The PDA medium amended with soil samples affected fungal radial growth, reduced FOL sporulation (23.53%-62.75%), enhanced TH (5.4%-9.3%) and VD (27.5%-41.37%) conidia production, and showed a slight effect (-2.00% to 4.2%) on SM microsclerotia formation. In ½PDB liquid cultures, almost all soil samples affected biomass production, decreased VD (85.02%-90.86%) and TH (20.01%-70.23%) conidia production, and increased FOL (35.13%-88.16%) sporulation. The SM strain failed to produce microsclerotia in any of the tested liquid media. Soil samples in the liquid media also affected the TH antagonistic activity mediated by secondary metabolites. The Pearson correlation coefficient linked the biological effects to PTCREEs and PTCREEs+TMs. The data recommend more frequent soil surveys to assess the impact of REEs on biota, especially at sites of naturalistic, geological, or tourist interest and sites of urban/suburban development. [IMPORTANCE] Toxic metals (TMs) and rare earth elements (REEs) can be essential or beneficial. Still, they can also become toxic to living organisms and pose a serious threat to global health, food security, and agricultural production. This study tests the effects of "naturally" contaminated sources of pollutants (TMs and RREs) in former bauxite mines on the biological parameters of three phytopathogenic fungi and one biological control agent (BCA) useful as indicators. The work also reveals the biological effects of naturally polluted soil on soilborne fungi, as well as a possible ecological implication of REE elements in former bauxite mines. Soil pollutants, REE in particular, could affect growth, dispersal, and ecological interactions of the microbiome, rhizosphere, symbionts, plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria, mycorrhizal fungi, endophytic bacteria, actinomycetes, nematodes, protozoans, soilborne agents of plant disease, and BCAs, as well as their development and ability to cause plant disease, plant protection, and human health.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Antibiotic heteroresistance observed across commensal Lactobacillus species.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Lactobacilli are prevalent members of the microbiota in the intestinal and reproductive tracts of humans and other species. They are commonly used in probiotics due to their beneficial effects on human health, including their association with protection from numerous chronic diseases. In addition, these microbes are often prescribed to maintain their presence in the host during antibiotic therapy, as well as to treat diarrhea caused by antibiotics. Despite many studies examining the beneficial effects of lactobacilli, less is known about how they survive during antibiotic treatment, and in particular, whether they exhibit heteroresistance, a phenotype in which only a minor subpopulation of resistant cells coexists with a majority susceptible population. Here, we tested representative Lactobacillus species for heteroresistance to a broad panel of relevant antibiotics. The results demonstrate that Lactobacillus strains, including those isolated from human feces, can exhibit heteroresistance to relevant antibiotics from distinct classes, and are often heteroresistant to fluoroquinolones. In particular, heteroresistance to fluoroquinolones was even observed in Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, a widely used probiotic. These findings significantly impact our understanding of how lactobacilli, including strains isolated from human samples, can survive antibiotic treatment, and how individual probiotic strains may be selected for use during antibiotic therapy to promote their survival and maximize their benefits. [IMPORTANCE] Commensal bacteria, such as Lactobacillus species, are widely used for their beneficial effects on gastrointestinal health and their potential to help restore the gut microbial community after antibiotic use. However, the antibiotic resistance profiles of these beneficial bacteria have received limited attention despite their relevance to probiotic use. Heteroresistance is a phenomenon in which a small subpopulation of resistant bacteria within an otherwise susceptible community survives antibiotic exposure, but it is often undetected, underappreciated, and has largely not been investigated among commensal bacteria. Our study provides a characterization of heteroresistance across distinct Lactobacillus species and a panel of antibiotics, revealing that heteroresistance is far more widespread than previously appreciated, especially to fluoroquinolones. These findings suggest probiotic strains could be selected that would survive concurrent antibiotic therapy and thus highlight that more comprehensive resistance profiling of probiotic bacteria may yield benefits to patients.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: Computational immunogenicity prediction for mRNA vaccines: benchmarks, bottlenecks, and the peptide-nucleotide gap
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractComputational prediction of T-cell epitopes has become indispensable to vaccine design, yet the field still relies on the assumption that how much of a given antigen is produced is fixed by its coding sequence. However, this is not the case with mRNA vaccines, i.e. the design of the mRNA template can vastly alter the quantity of the same protein produced. Codon usage, guanine-cytosine (GC) content, untranslated-region (UTR) design, and predicted secondary structure together define how fast the message is translated and how long it survives, and therefore how much antigen ever reaches the presentation pathway. This is a variable that no current immunogenicity predictor represents. Herein we appraise three decades of computational immunogenicity prediction, tracing the path from position-specific scoring matrices through pan-specific neural networks to transformer-based protein language models, and we use that history to expose the peptide-nucleotide gap between these tools and the way mRNA vaccines are designed. A structured synthesis of published evaluations of leading predictors across human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles, peptide lengths and data types shows that headline accuracy masks persistent deficiencies in predicting major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II, which underpins durable T-cell help, and rare alleles, which disproportionately affect under-represented populations. Four bottlenecks continue to constrain the field: class II prediction, T-cell receptor (TCR) recognition, immunodominance, and the disconnection between nucleotide-level design and peptide-level prediction. We argue that the last of these, which has drawn the least attention, is, in our assessment, the most likely to yield near-term gains for personalised cancer vaccines and pandemic preparedness, and we set out an architecture that couples translation-rate prediction to peptide presentation. Building it will require data that do not yet exist; we specify what must be measured, and on which platforms.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: G4SAINT enables interpretable prediction of RNA G-quadruplex binding proteins across the human proteome via domain-guided learning
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractRNA G-quadruplexes (RG4s) are noncanonical four-stranded RNA structures that regulate post-transcriptional processes and are linked to multiple diseases, yet identifying their binding proteins remains experimentally challenging and computationally limited. Here, we present G4SAINT, a deep learning framework that predicts RG4-binding potential directly from protein sequence, structural, and domain-guided features. G4SAINT integrates residue-level embeddings from protein language models with graph neural networks and domain-guided attention to capture complementary signals across modalities. Across multiple benchmarks, G4SAINT outperforms existing approaches and accurately highlights regions associated with RG4 recognition. By leveraging multi-task learning across related binding prediction tasks, it enables scalable application to large, uncharacterized human proteomes. Overall, G4SAINT provides a robust and extensible approach for systematic discovery of RG4-binding proteins, offering new opportunities for understanding RNA–protein interactions and identifying potential therapeutic targets. Our code and datasets are available at: https://github.com/o-nwn-o/G4SAINT.

Molecular Biology and Evolution.title: Tools for in vivo assessment of the intestinal epithelial barrier in inflammatory bowel disease: a systematic review
Molecular Biology and Evolution.abstract: AbstractBackground and Aims: Epithelial barrier alterations contribute to the pathogenesis and progression of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Barrier healing may predict long-term outcomes more accurately than endoscopic, histological or even transmural healing, and persistent epithelial abnormalities despite mucosal healing may underlie residual symptoms. Reliable tools are therefore needed to determine whether this therapeutic goal has been achieved and to support the development of barrier-directed therapies. We systematically reviewed the methods available to assess intestinal epithelial barrier structure and function in IBD.Methods: MEDLINE and Scopus were searched to July 25, 2025, for studies assessing epithelial barrier structure or function in patients with IBD. Animal, in vitro and ex vivo studies, and those without a clearly described assessment method, were excluded. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data on tools, thresholds, and associations with disease activity, treatment and outcomes.Results: Of 12 307 records screened, 124 studies were included: 73 evaluated permeability probes, 30 endogenous biomarkers and 25 invasive techniques, with four studies assessing both permeability probes and endogenous biomarkers. Probe-based testing relies on urinary recovery of orally administered sugars, polyethylene glycols, iohexol, radiolabelled compounds or fluorophores. Biomarkers reflect epithelial injury, microbial translocation, or the host response to it. Invasive techniques allow real-time, segment-specific assessment, principally probe-based confocal laser endomicroscopy, whose scores predict relapse and major adverse outcomes; endocytoscopy combined with multispectral spatial imaging is an emerging alternative.Conclusions: A broad range of functional, molecular and morphological tools is now available. Validating thresholds, standardising outcome measures and better defining barrier healing are the next steps before it can become a therapeutic target.

Science Bulletin.title: Lewis acid-base chemistry enables ultrastable zinc iodine battery through overall iodine species management.
Science Bulletin.abstract: Managing the complex iodine species (I2, I-, and I3-) with their conflicting chemisorption preferences and sluggish conversion kinetics remains a critical challenge in aqueous zinc-iodine batteries. Herein, we address this challenge by activating a pair of Lewis acid-base active sites (B/N) that enable specific chemisorption of each iodine species, effectively suppress the polyiodide shuttle effect, and simultaneously enhance the conversion kinetics between I2/I-. As proof of concept, a B/N co-doped porous carbon (NBC) host was successfully synthesized via a simple co-pyrolysis strategy. In situ spectroscopic analyses, electrochemical tests, and theoretical calculations collectively reveal, at the molecular level, that the Lewis acid-base active site in NBC reduces the activation energy for the iodine redox reaction and accelerates the conversion kinetics. Consequently, the NBC/I2 cathode delivers a rate capacity of 139.4 mA h g-1 at 5.0 A g-1 along with stable cycling performance of 139.8 mA h g-1 at 1.0 A g-1 over 1000 cycles under iodine loading of 6.0 mg cm2, as well as a low self-discharge performance. This work systematically elucidates the role of Lewis acid-base sites in the full-process management of iodine species and provides a perspective for designing highly catalytic host materials in conversion-type energy storage systems.

Water Research.title: A double-edged sword in hybrid nature-based systems: TiO(2)-driven PFOA defluorination and secondary resistome risks in bioelectrochemical floating beds.
Water Research.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, particularly perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), pose severe challenges for surface water remediation. While microbial fuel cell-coupled ecological floating beds (MFC-EFBs) offer a passive treatment strategy, inefficient electron transfer hinders recalcitrant C-F bond cleavage, often causing system inhibition under toxic stress. This study demonstrates that integrating TiO2-modified cathodes effectively mitigates PFOA-induced inhibition and restores MFC-EFB performance. TiO2 enhanced conventional pollutant removal, increased biopower generation by 25.1%, and achieved a 64.8% total PFOA removal efficiency (a 20.3% absolute increase over the control) via coupled adsorption, phytoaccumulation, and bio-photocatalytic degradation. These improvements are attributed to superior redox kinetics and photocatalytic activity, which alleviated plant oxidative stress and restored rhizospheric microbial diversity. Metagenomic analysis indicated a shift in microbial functional potential from stress-defense-associated functions toward degradation-associated functions, accompanied by increased relative abundances of genes associated with PFOA transformation and C/N/P cycling. However, TiO2-mediated reactive oxygen species generation and accumulation of potentially mobile short-chain intermediates was accompanied by 1.2-3.0-fold increases in the relative abundances of antibiotic resistance genes, triggering unintended eco-genetic risks. These findings highlight that while TiO2-modified MFC-EFBs offer a promising strategy for PFOA mitigation, the engineering boundaries and secondary risks posed by transformation metabolites and resistome proliferation necessitate rigorous assessments.

Water Research.title: Long-term multimedia records and Hg isotopes reveal mercury declines in a karst lake system.
Water Research.abstract: Mercury (Hg) recovery in karst regions is shaped by atmospheric inputs, watershed transport, and legacy contamination, yet coordinated long-term evidence across environmental compartments remains limited. We integrated records of atmospheric total gaseous Hg (TGM) and particulate-bound Hg (PBM), lake-water total Hg (THg), a dated sediment core, and Hg isotope source apportionment to evaluate long-term Hg changes in the Guiyang-Hongfeng Lake karst system, southwestern China. TGM declined by 69% from 2013 to 2024, available PBM observations decreased by 96% from 2005 to 2022, and lake-water THg declined by 45% during 2018-2025. The 1958-2020 sediment record showed low Hg loading before 1980, rapid enrichment during industrialization, sustained high contamination from the late 1980s to the mid-2000s, and declining Hg concentrations and accumulation fluxes after 2008. Isotope mixing showed that industrial-derived Hg accumulation flux decreased by 57% after 2008. Although watershed soil erosion contributed 72 ± 8% of recent sediment Hg, its higher relative contribution mainly reflected stronger reductions in industrial and precipitation-derived inputs. Recent sediment Hg concentrations remained approximately 3.6 times the pre-1980 level, indicating incomplete sediment recovery despite broad declines in atmospheric and aquatic Hg. These results show that Hg recovery in karst systems is pathway dependent and that watershed-derived Hg can remain important as contemporary industrial inputs decline.

Water Research.title: Thermodynamic-kinetic insights into seeded-driven crystallization intensification of metastable calcium sulfate solution.
Water Research.abstract: Metastable calcium sulfate in sulfate-containing industrial effluents is difficult to remove using conventional treatment methods. To address this challenge, a seeded crystallization pelleting (SCP) technique was developed to intensify calcium sulfate crystallization and facilitate solid-liquid separation. The effects of specialized seeds on the SCP process were investigated by combining induction-time measurements, classical nucleation theory (CNT) analysis, isothermal titration calorimetry, a multiple-binding equilibrium model, molecular simulations, and solid-phase characterization. Seed addition shortened the apparent induction time, enhanced sulfate removal, and promoted the formation of crystallized pellets. A thermodynamic-kinetic framework was used to evaluate separately the supersaturation-dependent nucleation behavior, the apparent contact-angle contribution to the heterogeneous nucleation barrier, and the thermodynamics of Ca2+-SO42- association before nucleation. The calculated apparent entropy change associated with pre-nucleation ion association increased from 0.04225 kJ·mol-1K-1 without seeds to 0.07481 kJ·mol-1K-1 under the seeded condition. The resulting increase in the favorable entropy contribution made the term more negative and contributed to a lower Gibbs free-energy change. Molecular simulations further indicated Ca2+-SO42- association and hydration-shell rearrangement in the bulk solution. Overall, the results demonstrate that specialized seeds enhance calcium sulfate crystallization through combined thermodynamic and kinetic effects. Heterogeneous nucleation at favorable interfacial sites, seeded growth, and attachment of fine crystallites may all contribute to the observed enhancement.

Water Research.title: Solar-driven evapofiltration enables co-production of lithium and freshwater from extreme brines.
Water Research.abstract: Recovering lithium and freshwater from brines could help meet lithium demand while providing a local water source in arid regions. Here, we present evapofiltration, a solar-driven process integrating a nanofiltration membrane with a carbon-nanotube photothermal layer. The membrane preferentially transports lithium over magnesium, while interfacial evaporation concentrates permeating salts and supplies water vapor for freshwater recovery by condensation. Feed recirculation mitigates concentration polarization on the feed side, supporting stable operation in concentrated brines. In simulated Dead Sea brine, multistage evapofiltration increased the Li⁺/Mg²⁺ mass ratio by 320-fold; subsequent purification and precipitation yielded Li₂CO₃ with 99.58% purity. An experimentally informed artificial-intelligence framework combines brine chemistry and solar irradiance to estimate lithium-recovery performance and evaporation rates across global brine resources. These results establish evapofiltration as a proof of concept for lithium and freshwater co-production through coupled ion-selective transport and water phase change.

Water Research.title: Integrating Ti-engineered LiMn(2)O(4) self-supported electrodes with flow-enabled ion transport for highly selective lithium recovery from brines.
Water Research.abstract: Electrochemical selective lithium recovery from brines is hindered by the low Li+ concentration, large Mg2+/Li+ ratios, and transport limitations within porous intercalation electrodes. Here, Ti-engineered LiMn2O4 nanosheets were grown directly on porous titanium-fiber felt (LTMO@TFF) and integrated into a flow-through capacitive deionization system. Control experiments distinguished the contributions of Ti incorporation, the binder-free electrode architecture, and the hydraulic configuration. Ti incorporation reduced electrochemical polarization and favored Li⁺ intercalation, while direct growth on the conductive substrate improved electrical coupling and active-site accessibility. Flow-through operation introduced convective transport within the porous electrode, alleviating solution-phase mass-transfer limitations without substantially changing the intrinsic charge-transfer resistance. LTMO@TFF delivers an exceptional lithium adsorption capacity of 5.43 mmol g-1 and an ultrafast adsorption rate of 1.34 mmol g-1 min-1, with a low energy consumption of 0.35 KWh Kg-1. Density functional theory calculations reveal that Ti incorporation lowers the Li+ intercalation energy barrier (-4.13 eV) compared with pristine LiMn2O4 (-3.75 eV), accounting for the improved kinetics. Moreover, LTMO@TFF achieves outstanding cycling stability with 92.2% capacity retention after 1000 galvanostatic charge-discharge cycles. Such superior performance stems from the Ti-induced reinforcement of the [MnO6] octahedral framework, which effectively suppresses the Jahn-Teller distortion associated with Mn3+. Consequently, LTMO@TFF exhibits enhanced redox reversibility and remarkable Li+ selectivity in both model electrolytes and real Dongtai Jinaier salt lake brine, achieving a separation factor of 43.6 in brines with a Mg2+/Li+ ratio of 20. These results demonstrate that coordinating electrode-scale insertion kinetics with reactor-scale liquid transport can improve lithium recovery from complex brines.

Water Research.title: Antagonistic-type non-additive shifts of groundwater nitrogen cycling patterns in coastal aquifers exposed to low-concentration multi-contaminant mixtures.
Water Research.abstract: Human activities and seawater intrusion promote salinity-ammonium enrichment and contaminant co-occurrence in coastal groundwater, yet their joint associations with nitrogen-cycling genetic potential remain unclear. We studied a coastal industrial aquifer (Cl-: 816-20,570 mg/L; NH4+-N: up to 19.0 mg/L) containing arsenic (As), fluoride (F-), volatile phenols (VPs), and total petroleum hydrocarbons (TPH) at concentrations far below salinity-ammonium background levels. We combined hydrochemistry, nitrate isotopes, metagenomics, and additive-null modeling to characterize nitrogen-cycling gene profiles across water types and associations with groundwater contaminants. Relative to river and seawater, groundwater showed stronger, more complex nitrogen-transformation genetic potential. Along the salinity-ammonium gradient, nitrate-reduction and nitrogen-retention genes were more prominent, while nitrification and nitrogen-removal potential persisted. After adjusting salinity-ammonium background, As, F-, VPs, and TPH showed differential associations across nitrogen-cycling modules, suggesting differentiated perturbation of genetic potential. Arsenic showed broad concentration-related signals and As-N gene-matrix covariation (RV = 0.653). Additive-null analysis (Bmean model) showed an antagonistic-type negative deviation (Δ = -0.063, P = 0.17, bootstrap 95% CI: -0.363 to 0.126). While As (0.012) and F--TPH-VPs (0.042) individually showed positive estimates, their combined estimate turned negative (-0.008), further showing a reversal-type tendency. The BPC1 model also yielded a negative deviation (Δ = -0.125, P = 0.05, 95% CI: -0.481 to 0.030); leave-one-out estimates remained negative in both models. These results show an antagonistic-type non-additive shift. These findings reveal two contaminant-associated influences superimposed on the salinity-ammonium hydrogeochemical background: cross-module functional perturbation and aggregate non-additivity, informing nitrogen-fate and natural-attenuation assessment.

Water Research.title: Granule size-associated differentiation in photogranular sludge systems: Linking granular properties, microbial ecology, and system function.
Water Research.abstract: Photogranular sludge (PG) systems offer a promising route toward energy-efficient wastewater treatment and resource recovery, yet how granule size is associated with functional differentiation remains poorly understood. Here, mature PGs were separated into three size fractions (<0.5 mm, 0.5-1 mm, and 1-1.5 mm) to characterize size-associated differences in granular properties, microbial ecological organization, and system function. Larger granule-size fractions were characterized by greater physical compaction, with lower pore volume, porosity, and permeability, together with higher surface hydrophobicity and mechanical rigidity. Paradoxically, despite the development of a denser and less permeable structure, larger granules exhibited more integrated microbial networks, stronger phototrophic-heterotrophic associations, and a greater importance of stochastic processes in community assembly. Variation partitioning analysis showed that granule-associated properties jointly accounted for 59.0% of microbial community variation, quantitatively linking granular properties with ecological organization. These ecological shifts coincided with elevated metabolic potential, reflected by higher abundances of key functional genes (narG, nirS, and ppk1) and enzyme activities. Consequently, the 1-1.5 mm fraction exhibited the highest specific pollutant removal rates, with DOC, TN, and PO43--P removal rates increasing by 20.3%, 49.2%, and 32.4%, respectively, compared with the <0.5 mm fraction. Resource recovery also showed pronounced size dependence: small granules maximized alginate-like exopolysaccharide production, medium granules yielded hydrogels with a more compact macroscopic appearance, whereas large granules accumulated the most lipids (39.0% higher than the smallest fraction) and exhibited enhanced lipid biosynthesis potential. Overall, this study establishes a size-associated property-ecology-function framework for PG systems and suggests that managing granule-size distributions may provide a potential operational strategy for simultaneously optimizing wastewater treatment and resource recovery.

mBio.title: Ribosome stalling activates a conserved quality control pathway in Archaea.
mBio.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Ribosome stalling caused by defective mRNAs or translational stress can generate incomplete polypeptides and compromise ribosome availability. Although ribosome-associated quality control (RQC) pathways are well characterized in eukaryotes and bacteria, their presence in Archaea remains unexplored. Here, we established a programmable ribosome stalling system in the archaeon Sulfolobus acidocaldarius and used it to characterize the associated quality control machinery. Stalled ribosomes recruit the conserved NEMF/Rqc2 homolog aRqc2 together with the ribosome rescue factors aPelota and ABCE1. Proteomic and genetic analyses further identify the kinase-ATPase Rio2 and a previously uncharacterized archaeal factor, aRqcF, as candidate components of archaeal RQC. Stalled ribosome complexes also associate with RNA-processing factors, the archaeal exosome, and the proteasome-associated machinery, linking ribosome surveillance to RNA and protein quality control. Finally, we show that a short C-terminal alanine-rich sequence is sufficient to destabilize a reporter protein in S. acidocaldarius, demonstrating that alanine-rich sequences can function as degradation-promoting signals in Archaea. These findings suggest that archaeal RQC shares fundamental features with bacterial and eukaryotic systems, supporting an evolutionarily conserved principle of ribosome surveillance and quality control across the three domains of life. [IMPORTANCE] Ribosome-associated quality control (RQC) is essential for maintaining proteome integrity when translation is interrupted, yet how this pathway operates in Archaea remains poorly understood. Here, we establish a programmable in vivo system in the Archaeon Sulfolobus acidocaldarius and use it to define conserved and archaea-specific features of ribosome surveillance. By bridging a central evolutionary divide, this work provides new insight into the origin and diversification of translational quality control mechanisms that safeguard proteome integrity. In addition, it establishes S. acidocaldarius as a versatile experimental model for investigating archaeal RQC and its evolution.

mBio.title: Spatial and molecular control of HIV-1 assembly and budding.
mBio.abstract: Combination antiretroviral therapy has transformed HIV-1 infection into a chronic, manageable condition, yet lifelong treatment remains necessary due to the persistence of latent reservoirs and the continual emergence of drug-resistant variants. Most approved antivirals target early entry or enzymatic steps, leaving the late phase of replication-Gag trafficking, lattice assembly, membrane scission, envelope incorporation, and protease-driven maturation-underexplored as a target for antiviral inhibitors. Recent advances in cryo-electron microscopy, cryo-electron tomography, single-molecule and live-cell imaging, and integrative systems-level approaches reveal that HIV-1 assembly and egress are not linear, virus-autonomous reactions. Instead, they are spatially and temporally coordinated processes embedded within host cellular architecture. Viral RNA scaffolding, plasma membrane composition and curvature, microdomain identity, cytoskeletal dynamics, and endosomal sorting complexes required for transport (ESCRT)-mediated membrane fission are tightly coupled to Gag lattice formation, establishing regulated checkpoints that vary across cell types and tissue microenvironments. This host-integrated framework reframes HIV-1 morphogenesis as a systems-level process and highlights structurally constrained, host-dependent nodes as promising targets for next-generation antiviral strategies.

mBio.title: Combination of environment-responsive growth and stochastic growth initiation shapes population establishment dynamics in the ammonia-oxidizing bacterium Nitrosomonas sp. PY1.
mBio.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Many environmental bacteria do not readily grow under laboratory conditions, and population establishment often occurs stochastically. Although the scout hypothesis has been proposed to explain stochastic population establishment in environmental bacteria, how stochastic population establishment is shaped by individual cell growth behaviors in environmental isolates remains unclear. Here, we focused on the ammonia-oxidizing bacterium Nitrosomonas sp. PY1 and showed that environmentally responsive individual cell growth behavior combined with stochastic growth initiation shapes both deterministic and stochastic population establishment. Replicate cultivation revealed that PY1 exhibited stochastic population establishment, whereas the addition of its own cell-free supernatant (CFS) induced synchronous population establishment. Using single-cell observations, we found that PY1 exhibited ΔVt-dependent changes in individual cell growth behavior, where ΔVt represents instantaneous biomass production per unit volume. These ΔVt-dependent changes were suppressed by the addition of cell-free supernatant, suggesting that cell-derived compounds in the supernatant may modulate individual cell growth behavior in PY1. An individual-based model incorporating ΔVt-dependent individual cell growth behavior could describe the synchronous population establishment of PY1 in the presence of cell-free supernatant. By contrast, describing stochastic population establishment in the absence of cell-free supernatant required the additional incorporation of ΔVt-independent stochastic growth initiation following a Weibull distribution. These results suggest that the combination of ΔVt-dependent cell growth behavior and ΔVt-independent stochastic growth initiation can lead to deterministic or stochastic population establishment in PY1. Such environmentally responsive changes in population establishment dynamics may contribute to the low isolation success of environmental bacteria and sudden blooms of the rare biosphere. [IMPORTANCE] Many environmental bacteria establish populations stochastically under laboratory conditions, but how individual cell behavior shapes stochastic population establishment remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the ammonia-oxidizing bacterium Nitrosomonas sp. PY1 using single-cell observations and quantitative modeling. We found that its own culture supernatant synchronized population establishment timing and altered individual cell growth behavior. Furthermore, simulations based on observed single-cell behavior could describe synchronous population establishment dynamics in the presence of supernatant. However, describing heterogeneous population establishment dynamics in the absence of supernatant required the incorporation of stochastic growth initiation. These findings suggest that understanding population establishment dynamics in PY1 requires consideration of both environmentally responsive cell growth behavior and stochastic growth initiation. This study provides a quantitative framework linking individual cell behavior to stochastic population establishment in environmental bacteria and may help explain the low cultivation success and sudden blooms of rare environmental microorganisms.

mBio.title: Receptor specificity and glycocalyx accessibility shape bovine P[1] and P[11] rotavirus infection.
mBio.abstract: Viruses initiate infection by engaging receptors within the crowded cell-surface glycocalyx; however, how this environment affects receptor accessibility remains poorly understood. Here, we compared two bovine rotavirus field isolates, P[1] C73 and P[11] HM26, which differ markedly in replication efficiency and early disease kinetics, to examine how VP4-mediated receptor use contributes to these phenotypes. Reverse-genetics experiments identified VP4, particularly its VP8* lectin domain, as a major determinant of the replication difference. C73 recognized sialylated gangliosides, whereas HM26 bound type II precursor glycans. Although HM26 VP8* displayed higher intrinsic affinity for its type II glycan ligand, it bound less efficiently to intact cell surfaces and was associated with lower viral attachment. Neuraminidase treatment increased the detectable accessibility of type II glycans, reduced P[1] infection, and enhanced P[11] infection. Structural modeling and mutational analysis further supported a role for VP8* residue 188 in the glycan-binding phenotype. The Y188T substitution reduced detectable glycan binding, impaired replication in the rBLR/C73VP4 background, and attenuated early infection in neonatal mice. Analysis of human P[1] and P[11] VP8* proteins also revealed an association between the Y/T188 polymorphism and glycan preference in the strains examined. Together, these results indicate that intrinsic VP8* glycan-binding affinity alone does not predict effective receptor use at the intact cell surface. Receptor accessibility within the glycocalyx also contributes to bovine rotavirus attachment and infection.IMPORTANCERotavirus infection begins with specific glycan recognition on the host cell surface; however, receptor presence alone is insufficient to guarantee productive viral engagement. Comparing bovine P[1] and P[11] rotaviruses with distinct glycan preferences reveals that receptor accessibility within the glycocalyx critically dictates viral attachment and subsequent infection. Notably, higher affinity for an isolated glycan fails to confer superior binding efficiency on intact cells. These results demonstrate that the glycocalyx acts as a functional barrier and modulator at the virus-cell interface rather than an inert receptor scaffold, underscoring the role of spatial glycan organization in governing viral entry.

mBio.title: mGem: A perspective on membrane-dependent regulation through the GraS sensor kinase in staphylococci.
mBio.abstract: Bacterial adaptation to host environments relies on the ability to sense and respond to chemical cues. In staphylococci, the GraRS two-component system senses and responds to antimicrobial peptides, acidic pH, and host-derived fatty acids, regulating pathways involved in stress resistance and virulence. Despite conservation of orthologous two-component sensor systems including GraRS, Staphylococcus aureus and Staphylococcus epidermidis respond differently to the same host-derived signals. We highlight emerging evidence that differences in membrane phospholipid composition may influence GraRS signaling by altering the biophysical environment of the sensor kinase. Because combined exposure to acidic pH and host fatty acids drives distinct membrane remodeling programs in these species, membrane composition may act as a key determinant of signal perception and downstream regulatory output. Understanding this membrane-dependent control of GraRS signaling provides a new framework for explaining divergent adaptations of commensal and pathogenic staphylococci to common environmental signals.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: PlanMine 4.0: an updated database for planarian genomics and transcriptomics.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: PlanMine is a web-based resource designed to facilitate bioinformatics analyses of genome, transcriptome, and gene expression datasets from planarians, free-living flatworms most well known for their large population of adult stem cells and extraordinary regenerative capabilities. This update incorporates high-quality genome sequences and annotations for multiple species in the widely studied Schmidtea genus, including both sexual and asexual strains of the model planarian Schmidtea mediterranea, while also expanding coverage of transcriptomes across the phylum Platyhelminthes (flatworms) to 70 species. New expression studies and tools are added to aid in the visualization and analysis of both bulk and single-cell RNA-seq data. Together, these resources will further empower complementary mechanistic studies in S. mediterranea and comparative approaches exploring the evolution of regeneration, parasitism, and other traits for which this increasingly tractable phylum represents an ideal model system. The PlanMine 4.0 database is freely accessible at https://planmine-v4.mpinat.mpg.de.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: The International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (INSDC): sustaining open sequence data at global scale.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (INSDC; http://www.insdc.org/) provides global infrastructure for the collection, preservation, and dissemination of nucleotide sequence data through its three member organizations. As the collaboration approaches four decades of three-way data exchange, continued growth in both the volume and geographic distribution of data is creating new challenges. Cumulative volume now stands at over 75 PB, having doubled approximately every 2.5 years over the past decade. Data reuse is extensively demonstrated by the 39 055 publications citing INSDC records in the 12 months to August 2026. The INSDC has established a new governance structure and a formal pathway for membership, supported by minimal technical specifications that enable independently developed systems to interoperate. Prospect members are now progressing through this pathway. The collaboration is also responding to an evolving policy landscape, which needs to be balanced with its founding commitment to free and unrestricted access. Looking ahead, the INSDC is exploring more scalable approaches to data storage and federation, strengthening approaches to attribution and reuse, and considering applications of artificial intelligence for metadata enrichment and submission support. Altogether, these developments aim to sustain an open, global, and interoperable nucleotide sequence archive.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: CoralDB: a comprehensive functional and evolutionary multi-omics database for stony corals.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Stony corals are foundation species of coral reef ecosystems, yet their biology remains insufficiently explored from an integrative multi-omics perspective. Although the rapid accumulation of genomic and other omics resources offers opportunities to understand coral evolution, development, adaptation, and symbiosis, accessing and utilizing these resources remain challenging. Here, we present CoralDB (http://www.coraldb.net), a comprehensive, genome-centered multi-omics resource that systematically consolidates multi-omics, evolutionary, ecological, and phenotypic data for stony corals and their holobionts. CoralDB covers 414 species and integrates approximately 19 421 datasets, including 12 data dimensions. Moreover, CoralDB offers valuable customized datasets and analytical resources, including standardized functional annotations, gene-family and pan-genome profiles, macro- and microsynteny analyses, spatiotemporal expression patterns, cell-type markers, phylogenetic resources, and symbiont-associated data. An integrated genome browser and interactive modules support flexible data querying, filtering, analysis, visualization, and links to public databases. CoralDB provides an accessible and extensible platform that will help the coral research community manage expanding multi-omics resources, accelerate discoveries in coral biology, evolution, symbiosis, and conservation, and facilitate deeper understanding of reef resilience under accelerating global environmental change.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: ERV Navigator: a unified evolutionary reference resource for human endogenous retroviruses.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) are genomic remnants of ancient retroviral infections that provide a record of host-virus evolution and contribute to the structure, regulation, and function of host genomes. ERV Navigator addresses a longstanding challenge in ERV research: the absence of a unified, evolutionarily informed framework that reconciles existing annotation systems, nomenclatures, and classification schemes. Existing resources provide complementary views of human ERVs (HERVs), reflecting different discovery strategies, biological objectives, and historical conventions, making comparisons across studies and integration of evolutionary and functional data difficult. ERV Navigator integrates major HERV annotation resources within a single, non-redundant reference framework centered on genomic loci and their evolutionary relationships. The database organizes information hierarchically, linking retroviral taxonomy, lineage-level reference sequences, and genomic insertions through stable, phylogenetically informed identifiers. Historical nomenclatures and annotations are preserved through explicit cross-references, enabling seamless navigation between legacy resources and the unified framework. The web interface supports taxonomic browsing, phylogenetic visualization, lineage and locus pages, genome browser integration, sequence alignments, and search tools. By combining evolutionary classification with genomic, structural, and functional annotations, ERV Navigator enables reproducible comparison of HERV loci while providing a flexible platform for comparative, functional, and disease-associated data. ERV Navigator is freely available at https://ervnavigator.fredhutch.org/.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: PRGdb 5.0: a multi-layered resource for plant resistance gene discovery and exploration.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Plant Resistance Genes database (PRGdb) 5.0 (https://prgdb.org/prgdb5/) is a major update of the PRGdb, designed to expand plant disease resistance gene resources within a unified web platform. The release incorporates predictions for 97 plant proteomes and adds 288, 315 new putative resistance-associated proteins, bringing the database to 874,967 candidate resistance proteins from 279 plant proteomes. The curated reference collection increased from 199 to 462 experimentally supported resistance proteins. To complement domain-based classification, the platform introduces an AI-assisted prioritization layer powered by the Deep Resistance gene Evaluator Model (DREM), a deep learning model that evaluates amino acid sequences to predict resistance-associated features. DREM provides an overall resistance score, domain-level probabilities, a Structural Confidence Score, and a composite prioritization score, assigning proteins to five prioritization categories. Furthermore, PRGdb 5.0 bridges genomic sequences with functional data by transforming gene entries into connected evidence hubs. Through dynamic API integrations, individual gene pages embed real-time external data, including STRING protein interaction networks, Reactome pathways, Expression Atlas tissue profiles, and standardized Gene Ontology annotations. A redesigned interface supports multicriteria searches with Boolean operators, bulk downloads, and a live literature news feed. Together, these updates provide a scalable platform supporting the workflow from sequence analysis to target protein identification.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: DIANA-miTED v2: an expanded microRNA tissue expression database with an integrated healthy-tissue reference atlas.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are post-transcriptional regulators of gene expression that exhibit tissue- and condition-associated expression patterns. Interpreting their abundance in disease or experimental contexts requires a physiological reference. DIANA-miTED v2 expands its uniformly processed and manually curated collection from 15 183 to 49 630 human small RNA-sequencing profiles spanning healthy tissues, cell lines, and disease states. To our knowledge, this is the largest such collection of human miRNA expression profiles assembled to date. It adds 16 746 Genotype-Tissue Expression V10 profiles and expands the Sequence Read Archive collection from 4142 to 21 843, alongside the existing The Cancer Genome Atlas collection. Expression is quantified for 2656 mature miRNAs, with harmonized metadata covering 96 tissues or organs, 437 cell lines, and 503 diseases. Healthy-donor coverage increases from 709 to 23 281, with 1471 tumour-adjacent-normal profiles classified separately. The database distinguishes primary tissues and biofluids from cultured and derived preparations. A redesigned tissue-centric interface provides a body-map picker, sublocation refinement, multi-miRNA and multi-tissue querying, cohort summaries, and descriptive longitudinal browsing. Co-expression capabilities include pairwise Spearman correlation and precomputed WGCNA modules, with 263 overview and 105 source/project-specific reference networks. Quantified counts, reads per million values, metadata, and query results are available through downloads and a REST API. DIANA-miTED v2 is freely available, without registration, at http://microrna.gr/mitedv2.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: DGIdb in 2026: an interoperable resource for the druggable genome.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The Drug-Gene Interaction Database (DGIdb; https://dgidb.org) is an open-access aggregate knowledgebase that normalizes and centralizes drug-gene interaction and gene annotation data from diverse therapeutic and biomedical sources. Since its previous update, DGIdb has expanded its data content and added new tooling to better support programmatic access and local deployment. This release updates existing sources and incorporates three new sources of interaction data, including annotation data from the Molecular Oncology Almanac, the PRISM Repurposing Dataset, and the Broad Institute Drug Repurposing Hub. To streamline data access for computational workflows, we have developed dgiPy and dgiR, Python and R client libraries that provide standardized access to the DGIdb API. We additionally now provide versioned Docker images and a public data repository containing current and historical DGIdb data releases in TSV and SQL formats. Together with continued improvements to the web interface, these new resources expand FAIR, transparent, and reproducible access to drug-gene interaction data in the bioinformatics community.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: TISCH3: an expanded resource for single-cell and spatial transcriptomics of the tumor microenvironment.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The Tumor Immune Single Cell Hub (TISCH) is a curated resource for exploring single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from the tumor microenvironment. Here, we present TISCH3, which expands the single-cell collection from 190 to 408 datasets and introduces 69 spatial transcriptomics datasets, bringing the total to 477 datasets. The 218 newly added scRNA-seq datasets span 48 cancer types, and the spatial collection spans 27 cancer types. Spatial samples are curated and processed individually, and single-cell references enable estimation of cell-type composition at each spot. The spatial workspace comprises six modules: Overview, GeneExp, spatially variable genes (SVGs), CellAssoc, Communication, and Downloads. These modules provide sample metadata and quality-control views, spatial gene expression maps, ranking of SVG, cell-type correlation and conditional intra-spot co-occurrence analyses, inferred cell-cell communication networks, and downloadable data and results. TISCH3 retains the single-cell analysis capabilities of TISCH2 and extends them to spatial exploration of the tumor microenvironment. The database is freely available without registration at https://tisch3.compbio.cn/.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: The mOTUs-db in 2027: linking taxonomy, genome-encoded function, and biogeography across environments.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: A molecular understanding of microbial communities requires linking taxonomic composition to the genome-resolved functional potential of member taxa. However, this integration remains challenging since representative genomes from cultivated strains are unavailable. Here, we present a new release of the mOTUs database, which extends genome coverage of underexplored environments and enriches its 3.9 million genome collection with functional annotations. Samples are annotated with a new hierarchical environmental ontology and geographic coordinates, supporting customizable sample grouping and biogeographic analyses, while links to MicrobeAtlas provide further insight into global taxon distributions. The web interface has new features for interactive exploration of samples, studies, and taxon abundances on a map. The integrated mOTUs command-line tool enables taxonomic profiling of metagenomes, comparison of user genomes with marker gene-based operational species-level taxonomic units (mOTUs) represented in the database, and retrieval of genomes based on identifiers, taxonomic labels, and functional annotations. A new API enables high-throughput programmatic retrieval of user-tailored subsets. Taken together, mOTUs provides a foundation for advancing microbial ecology through systematic integration of taxonomic composition, functional potential, and environmental distribution of taxa within one framework. The database is available at https://motus-db.org.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: GI-DB: a comprehensive variant database for exploring the extensive genetic diversity of the Indian population.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The Indian population, characterized by extensive ethnolinguistic and biogeographical diversity, is significantly underrepresented in global genomic resources limiting the development of genomic medicine in South Asia. To address this, ~10 000 genomes from 83 populations were sequenced as part of the GenomeIndia initiative (Department of Biotechnology, Government of India). Here, we present GI-DB (accessible at https://ibdc.dbt.gov.in/gidb/), a public resource cataloging 136 million high-confidence variants, including 44 million variants which are not present in other global and South Asian databases. GI-DB serves as a population-specific reference resource for genetic variation across Indian populations. It can support the interpretation of clinically relevant variations for rare disease, complex disorders, and pharmacogenomics. The database is structured to provide allele frequency stratification across tribal and non-tribal groups, biogeography, and ethnolinguistic categories. The interactive browser facilitates exploration of variants and genes of interest, offering detailed annotations from tools like VEP, ClinVar, and comparisons with global databases like 1000 Genomes, gnomAD, and GenomeAsia. Researchers can search using different modalities and access data programmatically. GI-DB is a foundational resource for genomics-informed public health and clinical genetics, tailored for the Indian population.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: scCVD: a comprehensive single-cell omics atlas of cerebrovascular disease.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Cerebrovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death and disability worldwide. Initially insulting the cerebral vasculature, CVD pathology engages the entire neurovascular unit, including endothelial and mural cells, astrocytes, microglia, neurons, and the perivascular fibroblasts and infiltrating peripheral immune cells. Single-cell studies over CVD have generated enormous scattered and heterogeneously annotated atlases, which never supplement an organized visualization and an integrated analysis. Here, we present scCVD (https://scportal.cn/sccvd), an integrated single-cell database of scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq data for CVD that characterises expression patterns and chromatin accessibility of CVD-related genes across diverse cell types and disease stages. The current release comprises 701 high-quality samples from four species (human, mouse, rat, and marmoset), encompassing over 4.68 million cells. All datasets were manually curated and standardized, with harmonised metadata covering disease versus control status, disease time points and experimental interventions. scCVD provides analysis modules for differential expression, functional enrichment, trajectory inference, cell-cell communication, transcription factor regulatory networks, and chromatin accessibility, together with interactive visualisation. scCVD also supports convenient data browsing and retrieval, customisable online analysis and batch download, facilitating systematic investigation of cellular heterogeneity and molecular regulatory mechanisms in CVD.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Propedia 26: an expanded and updated database of protein-peptide interactions for machine learning applications.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Propedia is a database of protein-peptide interactions. In this new release, we expanded the dataset to more than four times the size of the first version and introduced a comprehensive set of new annotations. We systematically analyzed protein-peptide complexes to derive predicted physicochemical properties, solvent-accessible surface areas, interaction energies, interface residues, and interchain contacts. In addition, we applied machine learning models to predict the potential therapeutic functions of the peptides. Propedia 26 comprises 93 151 entries, including 73 392 protein-peptide pair complexes (pep-pro) and 19 759 multi-protein complexes featuring a single peptide interacting with two or more protein chains (Multipro). We anticipate that this expanded and enriched resource will support the discovery and development of peptide-based drugs and biotechnological products. Propedia 26 is available at https://bioinfo.dcc.ufmg.br/propedia.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: P2CS-Web: an updated resource for comparative exploration of prokaryotic two-component systems.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: P2CS-Web (https://www.p2cs.org) links genome-wide two-component system (TCS) repertoires to protein domain architectures, genomic neighbourhoods, and sequence-identity clusters. The current release covers 392 075 bacterial genomes and 25 663 653 TCS-associated genes, including 12 517 906 encoding histidine kinases (HKs) and 12 774 395 encoding response regulators (RRs). HK and RR protein sequences are grouped into 2 931 715 and 2 479 169 sequence clusters, respectively, each represented by a single sequence. Genome, gene, and cluster pages combine these annotations with member taxonomy and local gene organization. An additional annotation layer applies 18 HisKA-like profile HMMs to HK candidates whose primary annotation lacks a HisKA domain. The resulting matches can be inspected against the original classification and domain coordinates. Genome and cluster comparisons, representative-sequence alignments, configurable exports, and a versioned API allow users to examine TCS diversity and download sequences and associated annotations for subsequent analyses.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: MetaboLights in 2027: public metabolomics data at scale.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Open data policies and data sharing in the metabolomics field continue to increase. MetaboLights (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/metabolights) is a global, open-access data repository for metabolomics and related fields such as lipidomics and exposomics, hosting experimental data and associated metadata across species, methodologies, and domains. Here we describe significant developments in MetaboLights over the past 3 years to improve data submission, access, and discovery, and strengthen integration of public metabolomics data with other omics data types. As of September 2026, the number of completed submissions to MetaboLights reached ~6900, and of those ~3400 were publicly released. Overall, 91% of datasets were generated using mass spectrometry and 7% using nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. A new submission workflow has been introduced along with significant improvements in infrastructure, such as a new data transfer protocol for very large datasets (Globus), a new home page, and an automated study validation framework, among others. We also describe current trends in reuse of MetaboLights datasets and in the field as a whole. Finally, we outline future plans towards better data submission and metadata capture, the coordination with other metabolomics data resources through MetabolomicsHub, and the planned activities related to AI (artificial intelligence).

Nature Genetics.title: Tracing genetic risk of neurodegenerative disease through variants affecting microglial function
Nature Genetics.abstract: Nature Genetics, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41588-026-02839-wWe combined pooled differentiation of 261 human induced pluripotent stem cell lines into microglia-like cells with single-cell transcriptomics, cellular phenotyping and CRISPR screening to trace neurodegenerative risk variants through to microglial function. This approach identified genetic drivers that influence microglial differentiation, migration and phagocytosis, including disease-relevant effects at LRRK2 and TREM2.

Nature Genetics.title: Optimizing phenotype scale improves genetic analyses in large-scale biobanks
Nature Genetics.abstract: Nature Genetics, Published online: 19 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41588-026-02826-1SIQReg is a data-driven approach for optimizing phenotype scale transformation that substantially reduces scale-dependent heterogeneity while preserving biologically plausible nonadditive signals and improving power to detect additive signals.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Deletion of the ribosomal protein gene rpmJ activates zntA transcription through a translation-dependent mechanism in Escherichia coli.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Bacteria tightly regulate intracellular zinc homeostasis by coordinating zinc uptake and efflux systems. Previous work demonstrated that deletion of the ribosomal protein gene rpmJ confers zinc resistance in Escherichia coli in a manner dependent on the zinc efflux transporter zntA. In this study, we investigated whether rpmJ deletion enhances zntA expression and explored the underlying regulatory mechanism. Under zinc-excess conditions, zntA mRNA levels were markedly higher in the rpmJ mutant than in the wild-type strain. Notably, the abundance of the 3' region of zntA mRNA was significantly increased in the rpmJ mutant, whereas that of the 5' region remained unchanged. Enhanced zntA expression depended on the native Shine-Dalgarno sequence and the N-terminal coding region of zntA, suggesting an important role for translation of the zntA coding region in this regulation. Furthermore, expression of ykgO, a paralog of rpmJ that replaces RpmJ in ribosomes under zinc-limited conditions, abolished the increased zntA expression and zinc resistance conferred by rpmJ deletion. Collectively, these findings suggest that ribosomes lacking RpmJ or YkgO enhance zntA expression through a translation-dependent mechanism, potentially involving transcription-translation coupling, and transcription elongation.IMPORTANCEBacteria must carefully control the amount of zinc inside their cells. Too little zinc impairs essential cellular processes, whereas too much zinc is toxic. This study demonstrates that deletion of RpmJ, the smallest protein of the large ribosomal subunit, allows Escherichia coli to survive high zinc levels by increasing expression of the zinc exporter zntA. Surprisingly, this increase depends on translation involving the N-terminal coding region of zntA. These findings suggest that changes in ribosome composition can enhance gene expression through translation-dependent mechanisms, potentially involving coupling between translation and transcription elongation. This study reveals a previously unrecognized role of ribosome composition in bacterial adaptation to zinc stress.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: PlsY couples glycerophospholipid metabolism to lipopolysaccharide regulation through YejM in Escherichia coli.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: In gram-negative bacteria, glycerophospholipids (GPLs) and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) are built from a shared pool of fatty acids and must be made in balance for the outer membrane to assemble correctly. PlsX and PlsY provide an auxiliary route to lysophosphatidic acid, a precursor of GPL synthesis. Either enzyme is dispensable, yet loss of both is lethal, indicating roles beyond GPL production. PlsX has one such role, preventing the accumulation of long-chain acyl-acyl carrier protein species that inhibit fatty acid synthesis. Here, we show that PlsY, a glycerol-3-phosphate 1-O-acyltransferase, has a regulatory function in LPS synthesis. We confirm that PlsY interacts directly with YejM, which, together with the adaptor protein LapB and the protease FtsH, controls both the abundance and the activity of LpxC, the enzyme that catalyzes the first committed step of LPS synthesis. Deleting plsY partially rescued the growth, antibiotic sensitivity, and LPS defects of the yejM569 mutant, which cannot sense LPS, but did not rescue other mutants with reduced LPS synthesis or defective LPS transport. Loss of PlsY also restored steady-state LpxC to wild-type levels in the yejM569 background. When fatty acid synthesis was inhibited, plsY mutants produced more LPS than wild type, suggesting that PlsY restrains LPS synthesis when fatty acids are scarce. These findings establish PlsY as more than a biosynthetic enzyme, placing it at the intersection of GPL metabolism and LPS regulation.IMPORTANCEThe gram-negative outer membrane is a formidable barrier that resists many antimicrobial compounds and makes these bacteria difficult to treat clinically. The barrier is made of glycerophospholipids and lipopolysaccharide, whose synthesis must remain balanced for the membrane to assemble correctly. Here, we describe a regulatory role for the Escherichia coli enzyme PlsY beyond its known function in glycerophospholipid synthesis. Our findings suggest that PlsY signals to YejM, a protein that helps control how much lipopolysaccharide the cell makes by regulating LpxC, a leading target for antibiotic development. This link identifies a new way that gram-negative bacteria balance production of the two major lipid classes required to build their outer membrane.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Salmonella enterica strains differ in the effect of AcrABZ-TolC mutation on cell motility and susceptibility to bacteriophage Chi.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] The rise in multidrug-resistant pathogenic bacteria has renewed interest in phage therapy. The lytic phage Chi is a broad host-range phage infecting Salmonella enterica, Escherichia coli, and Serratia marcescens. Chi belongs to the group of flagellotropic phages, which require a rotating flagellum to infect host cells. We previously reported that mutations in genes encoding components of the AcrABZ-TolC efflux pump greatly reduce Chi infection of S. enterica Typhimurium strain 14028S (serotype Typhimurium [STM] 14028S). Here, we tested and rejected the hypothesis that the AcrABZ-TolC complex is the cell-surface receptor for Chi. First, STM 14028S mutants with an inactivating point mutation in the AcrB pump displayed decreased susceptibility to Chi. Second, STM 14028S mutants of individual AcrABZ-TolC components showed reduced motility on nutrient soft agar, and a ∆acrAB-tolC mutant exhibited an over 80% reduction in the number of motile cells. Together, these results suggest that Chi phage resistance may be mediated by an effect on motility rather than by loss of a cell surface receptor. Additionally, deletions of acrA, acrB, and tolC in another Typhimurium strain, STM 4/74, and two other serotypes, Choleraesuis and Poona, retained susceptibility to Chi and had no apparent motility defects. Taken together, mutations in the AcrABZ-TolC pump caused reduced motility and, thereby, Chi infection in STM 14028S, but not in other tested strains. These results suggest that this pump is not a cell surface receptor for Chi. [IMPORTANCE] Phage therapy is of rising importance for combating antibiotic-resistant pathogens. Particularly, phages targeting structures important for virulence are of interest as they present an exploitable evolutionary tradeoff, as bacteria will likely lose virulence to become resistant to the phage. We previously reported that in Salmonella enterica Typhimurium strain 14028S, the AcrABZ-TolC efflux pump, an important virulence factor, was also required for infection by the flagellotropic phage Chi. We report here that this requirement for Chi infection is due to reduced motility of mutants, rather than AcrABZ-TolC being the cell-surface receptor. The reduction in motility caused by AcrABZ-TolC mutations in strain 14028S is not conserved across other strains and S. enterica serotypes, including Poona and Choleraesuis.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Anoxia selects for high-fitness biofilms and reduces antibiotic susceptibility in Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Antibiotic resistance is a growing global health crisis, yet resistance is almost exclusively quantified under aerobic laboratory conditions that fail to reflect the complex microenvironments bacteria encounter during infection. Many clinically important infection sites, such as airways of individuals with cystic fibrosis or chronic wounds, are microaerobic to anoxic. To address this, we investigated how anoxia alters antibiotic resistance determinants, hypothesizing that anaerobic metabolism might change the fitness effects and selection of resistance mutations. We used experimental evolution to propagate Pseudomonas aeruginosa populations for approximately 200 generations under conditions differing in oxygen availability (oxic vs anoxic), growth mode (biofilm vs planktonic), and tobramycin exposure (subinhibitory increasing to inhibitory concentrations). Subinhibitory exposure reduced susceptibility to tobramycin by 2×-4× compared to ancestral levels, with anoxic populations consistently having higher minimum inhibitory concentrations than oxic populations. Mutations in fusA1 and ptsP arose across all conditions, but mutations in amgS were only selected in oxic populations-indicating condition-specific mutations in response to antibiotics. Notably, mexT mutations were observed in anoxic or tobramycin-exposed populations. Anoxic populations exhibited significantly increased biofilm formation, reduced twitching motility driven by type IV pilus gene mutations, and greater competitive fitness. Together, these findings demonstrate that oxygen availability shapes the response to antibiotics in P. aeruginosa, with the anoxic environment selecting for reduced antibiotic susceptibility, higher fitness, and high biofilm-forming phenotypes. [IMPORTANCE] Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an opportunistic pathogen capable of acute and chronic infections that develop antibiotic resistance. One aspect of P. aeruginosa that makes it so challenging to treat is its metabolic versatility. We wanted to understand how growth in different infection-relevant conditions, specifically anoxia and surface attachment, would alter the evolutionary pathways of antibiotic resistance.
