We found that the mutations causing reduced antibiotic susceptibility to the commonly used antibiotic tobramycin were condition dependent. We also observed that adaptation to anoxia resulted in P. aeruginosa populations that had high biofilm-forming capacity and were highly fit compared to their ancestors. This indicates that anoxic infection environments can lead to P. aeruginosa variants with increased resistance, increased recalcitrance, and potentially more virulence.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: SpoIVA contributes to efficient engulfment through a cytoskeletal-like mechanism during Bacillus subtilis sporulation.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: During endospore (spore) development in bacteria, asymmetric cell division generates two transcriptionally distinct cellular compartments, the mother cell and future spore (forespore). Signaling between these cells leads to sequential and compartmentalized transcription, along with key morphogenetic events, including the phagocytic-like process of engulfment and the recruitment of coat proteins to the engulfing membrane. The SpoIVA ATPase is an essential sporulation protein that assembles into static filaments at the forespore surface during engulfment, where it functions as the basement layer for coat assembly. Here, using Bacillus subtilis, we reveal an additional role for SpoIVA during engulfment. Cytological analysis of a spoIVA null mutant (ΔspoIVA) revealed engulfment defects, such as septal membrane bulges and asymmetric membrane migration, similar to those typically associated with impaired peptidoglycan remodeling during engulfment. Engulfment defects were exacerbated when ΔspoIVA was combined with mutants known to impact engulfment progression and efficiency. Importantly, a spoIVA mutant (K30A) impaired for ATP hydrolysis and filament formation in vitro but partially functional for coat assembly in vivo closely phenocopies the spoIVA null mutant engulfment defects. Based on these data, we propose a model whereby SpoIVA polymerization at the spore surface, independent of coat assembly, plays a mechanical and structural role during engulfment, akin to the cytoskeletal proteins that drive phagocytosis in eukaryotic cells.IMPORTANCEEndospore formation relies on membrane remodeling to generate highly resistant dormant spores in human, animal, and insect pathogens. During engulfment, the mother-cell membrane migrates around the forespore in a phagocytic-like process, while the spore coat is simultaneously assembled. SpoIVA is widely recognized as the ATPase that polymerizes at the forespore surface to nucleate assembly of the multilayered spore coat. Here, we demonstrate that SpoIVA also performs a distinct function during engulfment that is independent of its role in coat formation. Cells lacking SpoIVA, or carrying a polymerization-defective SpoIVA variant, exhibit membrane deformations characteristic of impaired engulfment. We propose that SpoIVA polymers provide structural and mechanical during engulfment, analogous to the role of cytoskeletal systems during eukaryotic phagocytosis.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Peptidoglycan remodeling prevents antibiotic resistance during oxidative stress.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: The bacterial small RNA (sRNA) OxyS is expressed in Escherichia coli during oxidative stress. The sRNA OxyS enhances cell survival by controlling genes involved in the regulation of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and iron-sulfur (Fe-S) cluster formation. Here, we used the MS2 affinity purification coupled with RNA sequencing (MAPS) technique to identify new target mRNAs of the sRNA OxyS. Our analysis revealed a significant enrichment of mepS mRNA, which encodes a peptidoglycan endopeptidase that promotes cell growth. Our results confirm a previous report on the sRNA OxyS repressing the translation of mepS. We also found that an ΔoxyS background facilitates the emergence of mutations, conferring increased resistance to the last-resort antibiotics polymyxin B and E (colistin), but only in the presence of the target mepS gene. This suggests that the translation repression of mepS by OxyS could prevent mutations in bacterial DNA during H2O2-induced oxidative stress. Moreover, we show that adding the antioxidant thiourea or sequestering iron in the ΔoxyS background effectively reduces the emergence of resistance against both polymyxin B and colistin. These results suggest that reactive oxygen species (ROS), in conjunction with intracellular iron, play a key role in driving the emergence of antibiotic resistance. Overall, our work underlines a mechanism of antimicrobial emergence implicating oxidative stress, intracellular Fe, and cell wall remodeling in E. coli.IMPORTANCEThis study uncovers an underexplored link between peptidoglycan remodeling and oxidative stress responses during exposure to antibiotics. By elucidating how MepS and the sRNA OxyS interact in the presence of polymyxins and oxidative stress, our study suggests that MepS may exert an anti-mutator function. The repression of mepS translation by OxyS seems to limit the emergence of antibiotic resistance driven by DNA mutations. Together, these findings suggest cell wall remodeling and oxidative stress response pathways as promising targets to enhance antibiotic efficacy and limit the emergence of resistance.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Molecular basis for bile sensitivity of Escherichia coli with defective LPS O-antigen assembly.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: The periplasmic space between the inner (IM) and outer membranes (OM) of diderm gram-negative bacteria is densely filled with proteins and peptidoglycan cell wall. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is transported through this crowded compartment and then installed at the cell surface. While laboratory-adapted Escherichia coli K-12 strains produce a truncated "rough" LPS, clinical E. coli strains decorate rough LPS with an O-antigen (O-Ag) polysaccharide. At the periplasmic leaflet of the IM, WaaL ligates O-Ag chains onto LPS once it has transited the IM, yielding long "smooth" LPS molecules that are subsequently transported to the OM. Recent reports claim that periplasmic O-Ag chains in ΔwaaL cells disrupt cell envelope integrity to cause bile sensitivity. The presence of long periplasmic O-Ag chains is suggested to stress envelope architecture. Notably, this bile sensitivity is suppressed by disrupting OM-peptidoglycan interactions. Here, we show that even O-Ag repeat units trapped in the cytosol cause bile sensitivity that can be similarly suppressed by disruption of OM-peptidoglycan interactions, despite O-Ag never entering the periplasm. We show that stalled O-Ag chains cause bile sensitivity because they sequester a lipid carrier, limiting its availability for other biosynthetic processes, especially peptidoglycan cell wall synthesis. Indeed, providing more lipid carrier effectively suppressed severe bile sensitivity in ΔwaaL even while increasing the accumulation of long O-Ag chains in the periplasm. Our study clearly shows that periplasmic O-Ag chains do not inherently damage the cell envelope. Rather, stalled O-Ag biogenesis causes a detrimental lipid carrier sequestration that presents as bile sensitivity.IMPORTANCELipopolysaccharide O-antigen (O-Ag) covers the cell surface of wild-type Escherichia coli strains. These long molecules are made inside the crowded periplasmic space and must be accommodated in this compartment. Recent studies reported that long O-Ag chains are toxic molecules in the periplasm, stressing the cell envelope architecture to cause bile sensitivity. We demonstrate that long O-Ag chains in the periplasm are not inherently toxic and that short cytosolic O-Ag repeat units similarly cause bile sensitivity. The accumulation of these O-Ag repeat units or chains acts to sequester an essential lipid carrier, which causes bile sensitivity by impinging on cell wall synthesis. Our study shows that enteric bacteria are vulnerable when lipid carrier availability is reduced, making them more susceptible to the antibacterial effects of bile.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Diversity of bacterial degradosomes and degradosome-like networks.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Regulation of RNA pools in bacteria is a fundamentally important process to allow for survival and adaptation to changing environments. RNA degradation is an important piece of this regulation carried out, in part, by the core RNA degradosome, which is a multiprotein complex composed of ribonucleases (RNases), RNA helicases, and sometimes central carbon metabolic enzymes. In this review, we highlight the diversity in degradosome composition across all phyla of bacteria and the differences between stable degradosomes and the more recently recognized transient degradosome-like networks (DLNs). Additionally, we describe advancements in understanding the RNA targets and subcellular organization of degradosomes/DLNs. Importantly, we discuss the roles of RNA degradosomes/DLNs during physiologically relevant stress as well as virulence. Our review reveals the great diversity among degradosomes/DLNs and underscores the need to study a range of bacterial species in this field beyond traditional model systems.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Phage N4 uses a SAR endolysin-holin system for host cell lysis.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Bacteriophages (phages) cause active host cell lysis to terminate their infection and release progeny into the environment. However, some phages have systems to delay their lysis, and thereby increase progeny yield, in specific conditions: a phenomenon called lysis inhibition (LIN). Two dissimilar phages of Escherichia coli are known to exhibit LIN: T4 and N4. In T4, a multi-protein mechanism stalls lysis and maintains the LIN state in response to superinfection in a high phage population density. However, the lysis proteins responsible for T4 lysis and LIN are not conserved with phage N4. In this study, we characterize the phage N4 proteins involved in lysis by molecular and genetic means. We define the functions of the minimal gene set required for lysis through heterologous expression and complementation. Furthermore, by sequence comparison with a selected mutant library that does not induce LIN, we have identified genomic regions both within and outside the lysis cassette involved in N4 LIN. We propose a model where N4 lysis proteins that execute rapid N4 lysis can be regulated to induce LIN. Despite the lack of conservation with T4 components, our study suggests that direct modulation of lysis initiation may be common and provides a springboard for identifying similar mechanisms in other phages.IMPORTANCEPhages are viruses that kill only bacteria. To do so, they use lysis proteins to disrupt the structural components of the bacterial envelope. There are commonalities between the phages that infect bacteria with similar structures, but there are also interesting differences we can exploit to learn more about specific phages or their bacterial hosts. In this study, we characterize the lysis proteins of the E. coli phage N4. Our results suggest that lysis regulation controls phage yield in N4 differently than in the well-studied phage T4. Future studies on the relationship between lysis proteins and phage yield could provide handles to use this information for optimal large-scale phage production for clinical or industrial applications.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Siderophore-mediated iron uptake in cyanobacteria: current insights and knowledge gaps compared with model heterotrophic bacteria.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Iron is indispensable for most organisms, but it is often not easily available in the natural environments. This constraint has considerable impact on cyanobacteria, which require large amounts of iron to support several physiological processes, prominent among them being photosynthesis and, in some species, nitrogen fixation. To overcome iron limitation, many cyanobacteria produce low-molecular-weight, strong iron-sequestering molecules called siderophores, and employ specialized transport systems for environmental iron acquisition. Although these systems share similarities with those of well-characterized heterotrophic bacteria, our understanding of siderophore-mediated iron uptake in cyanobacteria remains limited. To date, only a handful of cyanobacterial siderophores have been structurally identified, and few genes involved in their biosynthesis, transport, and regulation have been reported, but a complete understanding of these processes remains lacking. This review first briefly discusses the well-established siderophore biosynthesis, transport, and regulatory systems of the model heterotrophic bacteria Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, as a comparative framework. It further discusses the current understanding of siderophore systems in cyanobacteria, highlighting similarities and differences with heterotrophic bacteria, species-specific variations among cyanobacteria, and major knowledge gaps. The review also discusses the ecological significance of cyanobacterial siderophores and their emerging applications in heavy metal bioremediation. Overall, this review identifies important directions for future research, including expanded structural characterization of cyanobacterial siderophores, deeper investigation of their biosynthesis, transport, and regulatory pathways, and improved understanding of their ecological functions and environmental applications. Addressing these gaps will strengthen our mechanistic understanding of siderophore-mediated iron uptake in cyanobacteria and its environmental relevance.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Secretion of the Francisella pathogenicity island effector protein PdpE requires components of both the Sec and Type IV pilus secretion pathways.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Francisella pathogenicity determinant protein E (PdpE) is a protein of unknown function encoded within the Type VI secretion system (T6SS) gene cluster of the Francisella pathogenicity island, a region essential for bacterial intracellular replication and virulence. We previously showed that PdpE is secreted by the bacteria via a T6SS-independent pathway, but the specific pathway involved was unclear. In this study, we investigated PdpE secretion in Francisella novicida and demonstrated that it requires components of both the Sec general secretory pathway and the Type IV pilus (T4P) secretion system. F. novicida possesses two SecB paralogs, and either of the two paralogs is sufficient for bacterial viability and for T4P-mediated secretion of chitinase and PepO enzymatic activities. In contrast, we found that both paralogs are required for T4P-mediated secretion of PdpE. Bacterial two-hybrid and pulldown assays confirmed interactions between these two SecB chaperones. Genomic analyses indicate that the presence of two secB paralogs is a conserved feature across the family Francisellaceae, including species that lack pdpE, suggesting that-while they have overlapping and partially redundant functions-the two paralogs have evolved to fulfill additional specialized chaperone and/or regulatory functions.IMPORTANCEOur research shows that pathogenicity determinant protein E (PdpE) secretion in Francisella requires components of both the Sec general secretory pathway and the Type IV pilus (T4P) secretion system, making it the first gene product encoded within a Type VI secretion system gene cluster known to use an alternative pathway. Although genetically linked to PdpC, PdpE's reliance on an alternative secretion pathway may offer insight into its physiological role. Furthermore, we show that dual SecB chaperone paralogs are required for T4P-mediated PdpE secretion by Francisella, and bioassays indicate a direct interaction between the two distinct chaperones. Genomic analysis reveals that possession of two secB paralogs is a conserved trait within the Francisellaceae family.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Neisseria gonorrhoeae: a historical model for host adaptation.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Research into Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Gc) physiology, genetics, and pathogenicity remains deeply shaped by its history. Long before molecular tools were available, early clinical observations, human inoculation studies, and initial vaccine trials defined the field's primary experimental questions and limitations. Key features of gonococcal infection, including restriction to the human host, rapid phenotypic alteration during culture, and the absence of durable protective immunity, were documented empirically decades before researchers understood their underlying biological mechanisms. As a result, contemporary gonococcal research has largely developed in response to these early empirical findings. Modern genomic and molecular studies have provided mechanistic explanations for long-standing clinical observations, turning historical paradoxes into defined areas of investigation. From designing vaccines that target variable surface structures to surveilling horizontally acquired resistance determinants, the questions driving current research directly continue the experimental challenges investigators identified.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Lipopolysaccharide precursor mutants disrupt unipolar polysaccharide adhesin synthesis and cell surface functions in Agrobacterium tumefaciens.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Agrobacterium tumefaciens is a facultative phytopathogen and causative agent of crown gall disease, capable of attaching to surfaces via a polarly localized unipolar polysaccharide (UPP) adhesin. The UPP is composed of two distinct forms, one characterized by N-acetylglucosamine residues (UPPGlcN) and the other by N-acetylgalactosamine residues (UPPGalN). Two genes with presumptive roles in dTDP-l-rhamnose biosynthesis, rfbA and rfbD, were identified in a transposon screen to be involved specifically in UPPGalN biosynthesis. Examination of independent rfbA and rfbD mutations validates the transposon mutant phenotypes, with UPPGalN specific defects observed as well as general attachment defects and UPP-mediated cellular aggregation across all rfb mutants. Additionally, despite retaining flagella, mutations in the rfb genes impart flagellar motility defects. Suppressor mutations that rescue the non-motile ΔrfbD phenotype disrupt the remaining rfb genes (rfbA, rfbB, and rfbC), the phosphoglucomutase exoC, and a putative glycosyl transferase ATU-RS21610. Single-deletion mutants in the dTDP-l-rhamnose pathway also have hallmarks of compromised outer membrane integrity, such as increased sensitivity to high-molecular-weight antibiotics and increased expression of target genes for the widely conserved ChvG-ChvI two-component system outer membrane stress response. Thus, defects in the dTDP-l-rhamnose pathway cause multiple cell surface deficiencies, resulting in outer membrane stress, impaired flagellar motility, defective UPP production, and irregular adhesion.IMPORTANCEBiofilms are clinically and industrially relevant in many different contexts, with substantial health impacts and monetary costs. Surface attachment and motility are essential components necessary for bacterial biofilm formation. Many microbes utilize specific surface appendages or structures to facilitate attachment and motility. This study probes the process of surface attachment and subsequent biofilm formation in Agrobacterium tumefaciens and has revealed connections between the creation of polysaccharide precursors required for biofilm formation and outer membrane functions such as motility and membrane integrity. These findings broaden our understanding of the complex interactions between outer membrane surface functions and how disruption of relevant precursor pools can have multifaceted impacts that may represent useful targets for new antimicrobial approaches.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Lysinoalanine crosslinking in the extracellular flagellar hook of Synergistota.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Bacterial motility is driven by the flagellar motor, a conserved macromolecular complex that enables cells to navigate chemical gradients. In spirochetes, motility depends on periplasmic flagella whose function is supported by a unique post-translational modification in the hook protein FlgE: a covalent lysinoalanine (Lal) crosslink between adjacent subunits. This modification has been shown to be conserved across the phylum and is required for motility. In spirochetes, Lal is thought to provide additional hook stability needed to meet the demands of flagellar rotation in the confined space of the periplasm and associated load of the wrapped cell body. Guided by a bioinformatic screen based on conserved catalytic residues required for Lal formation, we investigated the possibility that bacteria with extracellular flagella also produce Lal. Using a combination of biochemical crosslinking assays and high-resolution mass spectrometry, we demonstrate that FlgE from Thermanaerovibrio acidaminovorans, a motile member of the Synergistota phylum, forms Lal crosslinks analogous to those of spirochetes in vitro and in wild-type cell culture. These results establish the first example of Lal crosslinking in extracellular flagellar hooks and the first instance outside of the spirochete phylum. Thus, Lal crosslinking is more broadly conserved than previously appreciated and may represent a general mechanism for enhancing hook stability and function for extracellular as well as periplasmic flagella.IMPORTANCEMany bacteria employ complex rotary engines known as flagella to propel them toward nutrients or away from harmful environments. In spirochetes, motility depends on lysinoalanine (Lal) crosslinks within the flagellar hook protein FlgE to strengthen the universal joint of the rotating filament, which resides in the periplasm. This study shows that the same type of modification also exists in a bacterium distantly related to spirochetes, Thermanaerovibrio acidaminovorans, that contains more typical extracellular flagella. Using biochemical experiments and mass spectrometry, we confirm that its flagellar hook protein self-catalyzes Lal crosslinks, marking the first time this modification has been observed outside spirochetes and in extracellular flagella. These findings suggest that Lal crosslinking is more widely conserved than previously thought and may represent a general strategy bacteria use to reinforce their flagella. Because motility is closely linked to survival and the ability of bacteria to cause disease, this discovery improves our understanding of bacterial motility mechanisms and how it is maintained across diverse species.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Genetic basis of glycine and L-serine toxicity in Staphylococcus aureus and the case for glycine as an antibiotic adjuvant.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] The toxicity of the amino acids glycine and L-serine at high concentrations in bacteria was discovered decades ago. In this work, we used transposon insertion sequencing (Tn-seq) experiments to determine the genes necessary to tolerate excess L-serine, diglycine, or glycine in the human pathogen Staphylococcus aureus. Our results indicate that intracellular accumulation of specific counterbalancing amino acids-such as alanine in the presence of excess glycine-is the primary mechanism of resistance to amino acid toxicity. Consistent with this model, specific amino acid and peptide uptake transporters were required for fitness in each treatment; the peptide transporter DtpT was crucial for fitness in excess L-serine or glycine, and the alanine transporter AapA was necessary for fitness in diglycine. Tn-seq results also identified the cystine/cysteine uptake transporter TcyABC as necessary in excess L-serine, suggesting that both peptide and cysteine uptake contribute to L-serine tolerance. In addition to uptake mechanisms, glycine and diglycine toxicity is neutralized by D-alanine aminotransferase (Dat), which is required for D-alanine synthesis. The requirement for Dat and DtpT function-but not AapA-in excess glycine is explained by excess glycine inhibiting alanine uptake. Building on this finding, we found that combined treatment with glycine and the alanine analog antibiotic D-cycloserine was strongly synergistic in inhibiting S. aureus growth. Overall, our findings identify targetable mechanisms underlying excess amino acid tolerance in S. aureus, with implications for developing novel combination treatments using the accessible and biocompatible amino acids glycine and L-serine. [IMPORTANCE] Growing evidence supports the beneficial effects of glycine and L-serine supplementation in combating bacterial infections. Previous researchers have found that combining antibiotic treatment with high glycine concentrations has additive effects with many antibiotics, even reversing resistance to antibiotics in some bacteria. In vivo, activating glycine and L-serine metabolism heightens the sensitivity of bacterial pathogens to the host complement system, and studies of glycine or L-serine treatments show low toxicity and reduced inflammation in mouse and human subjects. This study reveals that glycine may be an effective antibiotic adjuvant with D-cycloserine, and treatment with glycine or L-serine could potentiate other drugs that target alanine or cysteine metabolism, respectively.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: PBP1A and LdtJ transpeptidase activities are crucial for cell envelope homeostasis and counteract the selection of colistin resistance in Acinetobacter baumannii.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: The multilayered cell envelope of Acinetobacter baumannii is an essential structure that maintains cellular integrity and protects the bacterial cell against external stresses and antibiotics. It consists of an inner membrane, a thin peptidoglycan (PG) layer, and an asymmetric outer membrane (OM) enriched in lipooligosaccharide (LOS), whose lipid A moiety is the target of colistin, a last-resort antibiotic. Although lipid A is essential in most Gram-negative bacteria, A. baumannii can survive without LOS through envelope remodeling, particularly in strains producing low levels of the bifunctional penicillin-binding protein PBP1A (encoded by mrcA) or in ΔmrcA mutants. Here, we identify a genetic and functional interplay between the LD-transpeptidase LdtJ, which generates 3-3 cross-links, and PBP1A, which catalyzes 4-3 transpeptidation during PG synthesis. We show that simultaneous inactivation of both enzymes severely affects growth, viable counts, morphology, and OM homeostasis. PG analyses revealed that the ΔldtJ ΔmrcA mutants display reduced overall cross-linking and shorter glycan chains, consistent with a weakened sacculus. Co-immunoprecipitation demonstrated that PBP1A associates with LdtJ, suggesting that the two proteins may act in close proximity during PG synthesis. Notably, ΔldtJ ΔmrcA mutants exhibited the highest recovery frequency of colistin-resistant, LOS-deficient variants compared with wild type or single mutants. Together, our findings indicate that 4-3 and 3-3 transpeptidase activities play complementary roles in PG synthesis and remodeling, contributing to envelope stability in A. baumannii, and that disruption of these activities favors the emergence of colistin resistance. This work further highlights the importance of PG remodeling in maintaining envelope homeostasis and suggests that proper PG cross-linking acts as a physiological constraint to limit the emergence of LOS-deficient colistin-resistant variants in A. baumannii, providing new insight into mechanisms that contribute to envelope destabilization.IMPORTANCEThe global rise of multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii represents an urgent clinical threat, driven by its capacity to withstand cell envelope damage and escape last-resort antibiotics such as colistin. Although peptidoglycan synthesis and remodeling are known to influence outer membrane stability, how these processes interact in A. baumannii remains unclear. Here, we identify genetic and functional interactions between two major peptidoglycan biosynthetic and remodeling activities, 4-3 and 3-3 transpeptidation, mediated by the bifunctional PBP1A and the LD-transpeptidase LdtJ, respectively. Disrupting these activities weakens the peptidoglycan, destabilizes the outer membrane, and increases the emergence of lipooligosaccharide-deficient, colistin-resistant variants. These findings highlight the importance of proper peptidoglycan cross-linking for envelope homeostasis in A. baumannii and provide insight into how disruptions in peptidoglycan architecture influence antibiotic resistance.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Structural and biochemical insights into isophthalate dihydrodiol dehydrogenase from Comamonas testosteroni KF1.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Isophthalate serves as a carbon and energy source for several microorganisms through a dedicated catabolic pathway, in which isophthalate dihydrodiol dehydrogenase (IphB) mediates the NAD(P)+-dependent oxidation of 1,2-dihydroxy-3,5-cyclohexadiene-1,5-dicarboxylate (1,5-DCD) to protocatechuate. Here, we present the structural and biochemical characterization of isophthalate dihydrodiol dehydrogenase (IphBKF1) from Comamonas testosteroni KF1. Enzyme kinetics revealed IphBKF1 catalyzes the dehydrogenation of 1,5-DCD substrate with both NAD+ and NADP+, exhibiting a ~4 fold higher catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) with NADP+. Crystal structures of IphBKF1 were determined in the apo form, in complex with NADP+, and as a ternary complex with NADP+ and the product 3,4-dihydroxybenzoic acid (3,4-DHB; protocatechuate) at resolutions of 1.5, 1.8, and 1.5 Å, respectively. Structural analysis reveals an NADP+-induced conformational change that facilitates cofactor accommodation and identifies key residues involved in NADP+ binding. Sequence and structural analyses highlight two conserved motifs, GXXXGXG and YXXXK, characteristic of the short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) superfamily. Ternary complex of IphBKF1 (NADP+ and 3,4-DHB) and molecular docking with 1,5-DCD suggests that specific active-site residues contribute to substrate recognition and underpin the distinct substrate specificity of IphBKF1 compared to other SDR family members. Based on structural insights and comparison with homologous enzymes, we propose a catalytic mechanism for isophthalate oxidation. Together, these findings provide a comprehensive framework for understanding substrate specificity and catalysis in isophthalate dihydrodiol dehydrogenases.IMPORTANCEIsophthalate is a recalcitrant aromatic compound linked to the environmental release of phthalate-based plastics and plasticizers. However, the microbial degradation of isophthalate is relatively less known in comparison to other phthalate isomers. Efficient bacterial utilization of isophthalate requires a coordinated pathway in which the cis-dihydrodiol dehydrogenase IphB converts intermediates into protocatechuate, a central carbon metabolism intermediate. Despite its importance, the structural basis of this transition has remained unclear. Here, we provide a comprehensive structural and biochemical investigation of isophthalate dihydrodiol dehydrogenase (IphBKF1), revealing the structural basis for cofactor binding, active-site architecture, and conformational dynamics leading to the selective processing of isophthalate-derived substrates. These findings provide a framework for the design of enzymes with improved activity and selectivity for pollutant removal.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Anabaena, a multicellular model for cyanobacterial cell biology and biotechnology.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Heterocyst-forming cyanobacteria (order Nostocales) are a monophyletic group of organisms that grow as filaments usually made of dozens to hundreds of cells (termed vegetative cells) that can perform oxygenic photosynthesis. Under combined nitrogen deficiency, some cells in the filament differentiate into N2-fixing heterocysts, which do not produce oxygen and, indeed, keep a microoxic environment appropriate for the expression and functioning of the N2-fixing enzyme, nitrogenase. Thus, in the diazotrophic filament, oxygenic photosynthesis and N2 fixation are segregated into two different cell types, vegetative cells and heterocysts, which require intercellular molecular exchange to feed each other with fixed nitrogen and reduced carbon, respectively. The current understanding of heterocyst biology, including regulation of heterocyst differentiation, which also involves intercellular signaling, is the result of studying mainly a few strains of the genus Anabaena. Here, we review the classical studies that established Anabaena as a model for the Nostocales and clarified the basics of N2 fixation in these organisms. Then, we show how molecular genetics came into the scene and how it was complemented by genomic analysis. This, together with the introduction of modern cell biology approaches, led to a renewed understanding of cellular differentiation and unraveled a system for intercellular communication that is unique in the biological world. In turn, the new accumulated knowledge on Anabaena physiology and genetics makes these organisms an excellent system for the development of new synthetic biology tools that will be crucial for their use in biotechnology.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: A transcriptional repressor co-regulatory network integrates iron homeostasis and mycobacterial stress tolerance to oxidative stress.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: A hallmark of Mycobacterium tuberculosis survival and proliferation within the host is attributable to the effective stress response of the pathogen against hostile environmental conditions. Although controlled iron (Fe) uptake and maintenance of Fe homeostasis are closely associated with intracellular survival of mycobacteria, the underlying mechanism that accounts for the interdependence of mycobacterial Fe regulation and oxidative stress response remains unknown. In this study, we discovered that Fe accumulation connects intra-bacterial redox environment via the phoP locus. Gene expression analyses coupled with genetic, biochemical, and transcriptomic studies uncover a distinct mechanism that utilizes Lsr2 and the virulence regulator PhoP to modulate transcriptional control of the major Fe storage protein-encoding gene bfrB. Remarkably, regulated expression of bfrB determines bacterial tolerance to oxidative stress and its intracellular survival. Although both regulators could independently influence bfrB expression, the most fundamental insights are derived from the inhibition of Lsr2 binding at the bfrB regulatory region of the phoP-KO mutant strain owing to Lsr2-PhoP protein-protein interactions. Building on these results, we proposed a model suggesting how Lsr2-PhoP interaction, or lack thereof, contributes to stress-specific regulation of bfrB expression. Collectively, these results uncover a key mechanism integrating Fe accumulation to oxidative stress response, an essential pathogenic determinant of M. tuberculosis.IMPORTANCEWhile the availability of Fe remains essential for Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection and replication of the pathogen in human macrophages, Fe may be harmful as it catalyzes the generation of toxic reactive oxygen species from products of aerobic respiration to induce oxidative stress. Although interdependence of mycobacterial Fe regulation and oxidative stress response has been reported, the mechanism connecting Fe acquisition and oxidative stress response is yet to be fully understood. Results reported in this study identify and elaborate on a new mechanism of regulation of expression of the major mycobacterial Fe storage protein, which determines bacterial tolerance to oxidative stress and impacts intracellular survival of the pathogen. We demonstrate that the virulence-associated phoP locus controls Fe accumulation and contributes to the intra-bacterial redox environment. The results uncover a distinctly different transcriptional control mechanism of the major Fe storage protein requiring a co-repressor-dependent regulatory circuit, including nucleoid-associated protein Lsr2 and the virulence regulator PhoP. Together, these results unveil a unique mechanism of stress-specific gene expression, which integrates Fe homeostasis to oxidative stress response, an essential pathogenic determinant of M. tuberculosis.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Contribution of PonA2 to biofilm and colony formation independent of its catalytic domains in Mycobacterium smegmatis.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Biofilm and colony growth create microenvironments that require coordinated localization and function of cell envelope components. However, the mechanisms by which membrane organization contributes to cell envelope organization during multicellular growth remain poorly understood. Mycobacterium smegmatis contains an inner membrane domain (IMD) at the subpolar regions of the cell that contributes to cell envelope synthesis. Prior research identified PonA2 as important for de novo formation of distinct plasma membrane domains during planktonic growth. PonA2 is a penicillin-binding protein with transglycosylase (TG) and transpeptidase (TP) activities involved in peptidoglycan synthesis. To investigate the role of PonA2 during colony and pellicle biofilm growth, wild-type, ΔponA2, the complement strain (cponA2), and catalytically inactive PonA2 variants (TG-, TP-, and TG-/TP-) were analyzed. Subpolar IMD localization was maintained in wild-type cells during both colony and pellicle biofilm growth, demonstrating that IMD localization is not exclusive to planktonic growth. Loss of ponA2 resulted in smooth colony and early pellicle biofilm architecture and was associated with reduced abundance of trehalose monomycolate, trehalose dimycolate, and glycopeptidolipids. ΔponA2 cells in colony growth exhibited shortened cell morphology and lacked detectable IMD localization, whereas ΔponA2 cells in pellicle biofilm growth retained bacillary morphology and subpolar IMD localization. In contrast, the catalytically inactive PonA2 variants maintained rugose multicellular architecture, bacillary morphology, and subpolar IMD localization similar to that of wild-type. Together, these findings identify a previously unrecognized noncatalytic role for PonA2 in maintaining normal colony and pellicle biofilm development in M. smegmatis.IMPORTANCEPlanktonic, pellicle biofilm, and colony growth expose mycobacteria to distinct environmental conditions that can affect cell-envelope organization and survival. Prior research has shown that mycobacteria form subpolar plasma membrane domains that support polar cell elongation in planktonic growth, but it remains unclear whether this organization is conserved in multicellular biofilm and colony growth, where cells experience nutrient and oxygen gradients and altered cell-to-cell interactions. Our current study analyzed the plasma membrane domain formation across the two growth states and showed that membrane domain localization is conserved, while the mechanisms required to maintain these domains differ depending on growth conditions. These findings suggest that mycobacteria use growth state-specific mechanisms to coordinate membrane organization.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Correction for Robin et al., "The CpxAR signaling system confers a fitness advantage for flea gut colonization by the plague bacillus".
Thank you to our recently retired editors Joe Bondy-Denomy and Tina Henkin.
The virulence regulator ToxT influences Vibrio cholerae motility through the expression of the methyl-accepting chemoreceptors AcfB and TcpI.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Vibrio cholerae is the causative agent of the human diarrheal disease cholera. Previous studies identified "hyperswarming" (HS) mutant V. cholerae with enhanced motility and decreased virulence factor expression, but the genetic basis of HS was unknown. Through whole-genome sequencing, we have identified point mutations within toxT, which encodes the master virulence regulator, as being responsible for the HS phenotype. These mutations are loss of function, and they eliminate transcription of cholera toxin and toxin-coregulated pilus genes. Using single-cell video tracking, these HS strains were also observed to exhibit enhanced motility/chemotaxis (increased speed and decreased directional change). Two methyl-accepting chemoreceptors (methyl-accepting chemotaxis proteins), AcfB and TcpI, are positively regulated by ToxT, and expression of both AcfB and TcpI within HS mutants restores wild-type motility. Moreover, a V. cholerae strain with a hyperactive ToxT (N106A) exhibits reduced motility (decreased speed and increased directional change), and knocking out acfB and tcpI in this strain restores wild-type motility. AcfB and TcpI localize to the bacterial cell poles, suggesting they incorporate into the chemotaxis arrays to modulate swimming behavior. Our findings demonstrate that the absence of the ToxT-dependent MCPs AcfB and TcpI is responsible for the HS phenotype, demonstrating a direct role of ToxT in the swimming behavior of V. cholerae.IMPORTANCEVibrio cholerae causes the human diarrheal disease cholera, and the master virulence regulator ToxT is responsible for the expression of the most important virulence factors, cholera toxin and the toxin-coregulated pilus, necessary for disease. Motility is also important for the bacteria to cause disease, and in this study, we provide evidence that ToxT also modulates motility, providing a regulatory link between motility and the other virulence factors required for the pathogenic lifestyle of V. cholerae.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Molecular mechanisms and regulatory networks governing Yersinia biofilm formation and host adaptation.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: The genus Yersinia includes three human pathogens-Y. pestis, Y. pseudotuberculosis, and Y. enterocolitica-where biofilm formation plays distinct roles in transmission and environmental persistence. All three species share the core biofilm machinery-the hmsHFRS operon, encoding enzymes for poly-β-1,6-N-acetylglucosamine (PNAG) exopolysaccharide production, and the c-di-GMP signaling controlling this production-but their regulatory networks and biofilm outputs differ. Transcriptional control of hms involves an integrated network that includes the Rcs phosphorelay (reshaped by rcsA pseudogenization), PhoP/PhoQ, EnvZ/OmpR, BarA/UvrY, Fur/Zur, CRP-cAMP, RovM/RovA, and multiple sigma factors. Post-transcriptionally, the Hfq-sRNA and CsrA-CsrB/CsrC systems modulate gene expression; the latter is directly validated in Y. pestis and Y. pseudotuberculosis, whereas its role in Y. enterocolitica is inferred from genomic conservation. At the translational and enzymatic levels, polyamines sustain Hms protein production, while redox signals govern the HmsC-HmsD disulfide switch, controlling diguanylate cyclase activity. This multi-layer architecture ensures that biofilm output is tuned to species-specific ecological niches. In host adaptation, Y. pestis transitioned from a foodborne enteric pathogen to a flea-borne lifestyle through key genetic events-acquisition of ymt, pseudogenization of rcsA, inactivation of y2909/y3389, and ureD-which are not shared with Y. pseudotuberculosis or Y. enterocolitica, thereby explaining their different biofilm-dependent transmission strategies. Studies in Caenorhabditis elegans have identified host O-glycosylation modifications as receptors for biofilm attachment. This review summarizes progress on the molecular mechanisms, regulatory networks, and host-adaptive functions of Yersinia biofilm formation and proposes future research directions to address knowledge gaps. Future priorities include the identification of c-di-GMP effectors, flea-specific signals, 3D biofilm imaging, and CRISPR-based detection.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: The evolution of Brucella as a model intracellular pathogen.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Brucella species are intracellular bacterial pathogens that cause brucellosis, one of the most common zoonoses worldwide. This review traces how Brucella, first discovered in the 19th century through investigations of human and bovine disease, became a modern experimental model system. Work on Brucella has illuminated how intracellular bacteria evade and adapt to host defenses and how they remodel host cell biology to establish a replicative niche. It has also yielded insights that extend beyond pathogenesis into bacterial cell envelope architecture and development. Though long regarded as a small, homogeneous group of mammalian pathogens, the genus has expanded in recent years as "non-classical" Brucella have been isolated from unexpected animal hosts, opening new opportunities to understand the fascinating host preferences and evolutionary history of these closely related Alphaproteobacteria. More than a century after their discovery, Brucella species remain versatile models for the study of intracellular infection, bacterial cell biology, and physiology, and the evolution of host association.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Anti-mycobacterial activity of phage-encoded lysterases.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Mycobacterium abscessus is a non-tuberculous Mycobacterium (NTM) that is often associated with respiratory infections in persons with cystic fibrosis. High levels of antibiotic resistance make M. abscessus infections difficult to treat, highlighting the urgent need for alternative therapeutic strategies. Mycobacteriophage therapy-treatment of infections with viruses that infect Mycobacterium hosts-shows considerable promise, but the narrow host specificity of the current mycobacteriophage repertoire limits this approach to personalized therapies. Here, we characterize the anti-M. abscessus activity of mycobacteriophage-encoded Lysin B enzymes (lysterases). Lysterases are serine-esterases that cleave the ester bonds linking mycolic acids to either arabinogalactan or trehalose in the mycobacterial cell envelope to complete the lysis process. In this study, we explored their ability to kill a spectrum of clinically isolated M. abscessus strains when administered exogenously. Six phylogenetically distinct lysterases were purified, characterized on the surrogate M. smegmatis, and their activity against a diverse panel of 24 M. abscessus clinical strains was assessed. The enzymes exhibit a range of activities against these strains, but most have broad-spectrum activity with only minor variations among the M. abscessus isolates. However, the activities can be quite potent, resulting in up to six orders of magnitude of reduction in viability within 4 h with one activity unit of the enzymes, and act synergistically with amikacin. Overall, mycobacteriophage-encoded lysterases show considerable potential for antimycobacterial control, especially for topical applications.IMPORTANCEMycobacterium infections are clinically challenging, and there is a high failure of resolving Mycobacterium abscessus infections using antibiotics. Mycobacteriophages show promise in treating M. abscessus infections, but there is substantial variation among clinical isolates in their phage infection profiles. Mycobacteriophages are unusual in coding for lysis enzymes-lysterases-that target cell wall exposed constituents, and these can have potential antibacterial activity. Exploring the vast sequence diversity of thousands of phage-encoded lysterases identifies a subset that was expressed, purified, and tested for their ability to kill a broad range of M. abscessus clinical strains. Lysterases with the broadest and greatest activity offer substantial potential for treatment of M. abscessus infection, especially where they display synergism with current antibiotics.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Environmental context defines the physiological contribution of the Tol-Pal system to cell envelope integrity in Acinetobacter baumannii.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: The gram-negative cell envelope requires coordinated remodeling of the peptidoglycan layer and outer membrane to preserve envelope integrity during growth and division. The conserved Tol-Pal system contributes to envelope maintenance, although the physiological consequences of its loss vary across environmental contexts and among gram-negative bacteria. Here, we examined the contribution of Tol-Pal across diverse growth environments in Acinetobacter baumannii. Loss of Tol-Pal did not cause a substantial population growth defect, and septal peptidoglycan incorporation remained largely preserved under standard laboratory conditions. In contrast, nutrient-rich media, conditions that alter osmotic balance, and a host-like environment exposed defects in cell division organization and cell morphology. Tol-Pal-deficient cells also exhibited modest but reproducible reductions in outer membrane barrier robustness, and disruption of the Mla phospholipid transport system further exacerbated these defects. Consistent with these phenotypes, loss of Tol-Pal reduced bacterial fitness under environmental stress and host-associated models. Together, these findings indicate that Tol-Pal contributes to outer membrane barrier robustness and that additional consequences of its loss become apparent under conditions that challenge the cell envelope.IMPORTANCEThe physiological consequences of disrupting conserved envelope systems can vary with the conditions in which bacteria grow. In Acinetobacter baumannii, loss of Tol-Pal has little effect on population growth under routine laboratory conditions but modestly compromises outer membrane barrier robustness, whereas specific environmental and host-associated conditions reveal additional defects in cell division organization and bacterial fitness. These findings highlight how environmental context shapes the physiological consequences of Tol-Pal deficiency and provide a framework for understanding why the contribution of this conserved envelope system differs among gram-negative bacteria.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Structural basis for ITP-selective hydrolysis by a CRISPR-associated Nudix hydrolase.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: The nucleoside diphosphates linked to moiety-X (Nudix) hydrolases are a superfamily of proteins defined by the characteristic Nudix box sequence, most of which are involved in clearing the cell of potentially deleterious metabolites and in preventing the accumulation of metabolic intermediates. The Nudix hydrolase associated with CRISPR-Cas-associated adenosine deaminases (CAAD) from Limisphaera ngatamarikiensis (LngNH) mitigates CAAD-induced toxicity by hydrolyzing ITP to IMP and pyrophosphate. Here, we determined crystal structures of LngNH in the apo form and in complex with ITP using catalytic mutants and validated key interactions by site-directed mutagenesis. The hypoxanthine of ITP is deeply buried in a hydrophobic pocket and engages a distinct hydrogen-bond network, whereas the triphosphate tail is coordinated by conserved residues and divalent metal ions. Together, these findings provide a structural framework for CAAD-linked nucleotide sanitization and suggest that CRISPR-associated Nudix hydrolases function as local self-protection modules that limit toxicity from noncanonical inosine nucleotides.IMPORTANCENucleotide quality-control enzymes protect cells from harmful metabolic by-products. Here, we characterize a CRISPR-associated nucleoside diphosphates linked to moiety-X (Nudix) hydrolase that removes ITP, a toxic noncanonical nucleotide generated during antiviral defense. Biochemical and structural analyses show how this enzyme specifically recognizes and hydrolyzes ITP while avoiding related cellular nucleotides. Our findings suggest that CRISPR-associated nucleotide deaminase systems require "self-protection" mechanisms to prevent damage from their own antiviral activities. These results expand our understanding of how bacteria maintain nucleotide homeostasis during immune responses and reveal an additional regulatory layer within CRISPR-associated defense systems. The structural framework reported here also provides a foundation for future studies of nucleotide sanitization enzymes in microbial physiology and antiviral immunity.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: EndD mediates butyrate-dependent toxin release and sporulation in Clostridioides difficile.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Clostridioides difficile is an urgent threat to human health. Current treatments for C. difficile infections (CDIs) are antibiotics and microbiome restoration therapy (MRT) for recurrent cases. However, antibiotics contribute to antibiotic resistance and recurrent CDIs, and the long-term sustainability and accessibility of MRTs remain to be determined. Since a dysbiotic gut microbiome is the primary risk factor for CDI, a better understanding of the interactions between C. difficile, the microbiome, and the host will aid development of treatments with improved precision. Emerging evidence supports that butyrate, a prominent end product of gut microbiome metabolism, is a key determinant of C. difficile pathogenesis. Notably, C. difficile releases more of its toxins (TcdA and TcdB) in butyrate-rich environments. Here, we demonstrate that butyrate-dependent toxin release is not driven by two previously characterized modes of toxin release (e.g., TcdE-dependent secretion or Cwp19-dependent autolysis). Instead, butyrate enhances the expression of a broadly conserved endolysin (EndD), which is responsible for butyrate-dependent toxin release. We additionally demonstrate that endD-dependent toxin release does not universally occur under all growth conditions, that its expression is dependent on the late-stage sporulation sigma factor SigK, and that endD enhances butyrate-dependent sporulation. Overall, our findings provide deeper insight into butyrate-dependent effects on C. difficile pathogenesis and set the stage for future work to better understand the molecular and genetic underpinnings of endD regulation.IMPORTANCEClostridioides difficile is a leading cause of infectious diarrhea. The gut microbiome-derived short-chain fatty acid butyrate triggers C. difficile to release its major virulence factors, toxins TcdA and TcdB. Here, we show that butyrate-dependent toxin release is independent of classical secretion or autolytic pathways and is instead mediated by EndD, an endolysin broadly conserved among C. difficile clinical isolates. We also demonstrate that endD expression is governed by the sporulation factor SigK and enhances sporulation, directly linking transmission and virulence. Uncovering how C. difficile couples metabolic sensing to EndD-mediated toxin release and sporulation advances our understanding of pathogen-microbiome interactions and highlights potential targets for non-antibiotic therapeutics.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Activation of the MprBA two-component system in Mycobacterium smegmatis under acidic and respiration-inhibitory conditions and crosstalk between MprA and KdpD.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: The MprBA two-component system (TCS) plays a critical role in Mycobacterium tuberculosis persistence and forms a signaling pathway with the alternative sigma factors SigE and SigB. Here, we demonstrate that the MprBA-SigE-SigB signaling pathway is activated in Mycobacterium smegmatis under multiple stress conditions associated with respiratory inhibition, including genetic inactivation of the aa3 cytochrome c oxidase, treatment with the bcc1 complex inhibitor Q203, hypoxia, high ionic strength, and acidic pH. Strikingly, acidic pH elicited the strongest activation of MprA-dependent sigE expression, suggesting that MprB integrates multiple stress signals beyond respiratory dysfunction. Deletion of mprB resulted in constitutive activation of MprA rather than inactivation, as evidenced by elevated sigE expression, increased MprA phosphorylation, and enhanced rifampicin resistance in an mprB mutant. Using CRISPRi-mediated repression and genetic deletion, we identified the KdpD histidine kinase, a component of the potassium homeostasis KdpDE TCS, as required for phosphorylating and activating MprA in the absence of MprB. These findings reveal unexpected crosstalk between KdpD and MprA. Expression of a truncated MprB lacking the N-terminal sensory domain abolished sigE expression under both neutral and acidic conditions, indicating that this domain is essential for sensing environmental signals and that the truncated protein behaves as a phosphatase-dominant form under the conditions tested. Growth analysis revealed that MprA, SigE, and SigB are required for optimal growth under acidic conditions, demonstrating the importance of the MprBA-SigE-SigB pathway for survival of M. smegmatis under acidic stress.IMPORTANCEThe MprBA TCS contributes to mycobacterial stress adaptation and persistence by regulating SigE- and SigB-mediated stress response pathways. Here, we show that the MprBA TCS is activated under respiration-inhibitory and acidic conditions in Mycobacterium smegmatis, suggesting that this pathway responds to environmental cues relevant to host infection. We also identify an unexpected regulatory relationship between the MprBA and KdpDE systems: in the absence of MprB, MprA can be phosphorylated and activated by the noncognate histidine kinase KdpD. These findings suggest that MprB phosphatase activity is critical for maintaining low basal MprA activity and preventing inappropriate KdpD-mediated activation under non-stress conditions.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Protein secretion by the type IV pilus machinery in Francisella tularensis.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Francisella tularensis is a highly virulent, gram-negative bacterial pathogen that causes the zoonotic disease tularemia. F. tularensis infects a variety of host cells and replicates intracellularly while evading and interfering with host immune responses. The molecular mechanisms that facilitate the intracellular replication and virulence of F. tularensis are poorly understood. The Francisella genome contains a set of pil genes that code for the assembly of surface fibers termed type IV pili (T4P). T4P are major bacterial virulence determinants, but the function of the pil system during F. tularensis infection and intracellular growth is unclear. T4P are closely related to the type II secretion pathway, and the pil system of a related Francisella species, F. novicida, was shown to function in protein secretion as well as pilus assembly. To identify proteins secreted by F. tularensis, we analyzed the F. tularensis Live Vaccine Strain (LVS) using bio-orthogonal noncanonical amino acid tagging (BONCAT). Using BONCAT in conjunction with proteomics, we identified candidate proteins secreted by the wild-type LVS, as well as candidate proteins whose extracellular abundance decreased in the absence of the PilF ATPase or the PilE4 pilus subunit. Using epitope tagging of selected candidates, we validated T4P-mediated secretion of the ChiA and ChiD chitinases and the KatG catalase by the LVS. These results further our understanding of the pil system and protein secretion pathways in F. tularensis.IMPORTANCEFrancisella tularensis is a highly virulent gram-negative bacterial pathogen and the causative agent of tularemia. F. tularensis lacks secretion systems utilized by other intracellular bacterial pathogens but contains pil genes that encode for type IV pili (T4P) and may also function in protein secretion. T4P are observed on the surface of all Francisella spp., but pil-mediated protein secretion has only been reported for F. novicida, which is not normally pathogenic in humans. In this study, we used bio-orthogonal noncanonical amino acid tagging to identify proteins secreted by F. tularensis, for which there is limited information. We demonstrate that the F. tularensis pil system is capable of protein secretion and validate T4P-mediated secretion of the ChiA and ChiD chitinases and the KatG catalase. These results will facilitate investigation of Francisella virulence mechanisms and may provide targets for therapeutic intervention.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Effects of sporulation in an extremely poor medium on Bacillus subtilis spore resistance, germination, and physical properties.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Spores of Bacillus species are metabolically dormant and resistant to many agents but can come back to life in germination triggered by a variety of small molecules; these spore properties vary depending on the conditions and media for spore formation. In the current work, we have compared the properties of Bacillus subtilis spores made in a rich medium and an extremely poor medium. Notably, spores made in the poor liquid medium had lowered resistance to wet heat and somewhat lowered resistance to hydrogen peroxide and formaldehyde. Spores made in the poor liquid medium also have an inner membrane (IM) that is more permeable and fluid compared to the IM in spores made in a rich medium. The poor liquid medium spores also germinated slower than the rich medium spores with several germinant receptor (GR) germinants but faster with the non-GR-dependent germinant dodecylamine. While the reasons for the latter differences are likely the more fluid and permeable IM in the poor medium spores, there were minimal, if any, differences between rich and poor medium spores in their levels of core water or CaDPA, two compounds that alone have major effects on spore resistance properties. These findings provide new information on the resistance and germination properties of spores of B. subtilis.IMPORTANCESpores of various Bacillus species can cause adverse effects such as food spoilage and some human diseases due to their resistance properties and ability to "come back to life" in spore germination. The reason for these effects has been commonly studied using spores prepared in relatively rich media, and there is a large body of literature on this. However, there have been minimal, if any, studies using spores prepared in an extremely poor medium, as was done in the current work. We believe that the findings in this work provide new insight into mechanisms of spore resistance and their germination.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Efficient septum formation is essential for chromosome segregation in Bacillus subtilis when SMC function is impaired.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) complexes play conserved roles in chromosome organization, segregation, and repair in all domains of life. In Bacillus subtilis, SMC is required for the segregation of newly replicated origins. To investigate whether other proteins function with SMC in this process, we performed a synthetic lethal screen with an smc hypomorphic allele (smc*) that is mildly defective in chromosome segregation. In addition to recovering previously reported genetic interactions of smc with parB and spoIIIE, our screen identified minJ and divIVA as essential in the smc* background. We show that the synthetic lethality between smc* and ∆minJ or ∆divIVA arises from defects in segregating the replication terminus. Importantly, deletion of minD, which suppresses the cell division defects of ∆minJ and ∆divIVA, restored terminus segregation and viability in the smc* background. These findings support a model in which proper septum formation promotes chromosome terminus resolution and segregation by enabling SpoIIIE-mediated DNA clearance from the division septum during cytokinesis. These findings highlight the interdependence between chromosome segregation and cell division.IMPORTANCEThe SMC complex plays a central role in chromosome organization and segregation in Bacillus subtilis, but the cellular functions that become important when SMC activity is reduced are not well understood. Using a hypomorphic smc allele, we discovered that mutations affecting cell division become essential when chromosome organization and segregation are impaired. Our findings support a model in which efficient septum formation enables proper localization of the SpoIIIE DNA translocase, which in turn resolves and segregates the chromosome terminus region. These results highlight the critical role of cell division in supporting chromosome segregation.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Acquisition of novel arrays via horizontal gene transfer rewires CRISPR-mediated defense in Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat (CRISPR)-associated (Cas) systems form the adaptive immunity of prokaryotes, conferring sequence-specific protection against genetic parasites. Here, we functionally characterized the type I-F CRISPR-Cas system of Pseudomonas aeruginosa ATCC 10145 (PA10145), which led us to discover the existence of an isolated CRISPR array unique to this system. Its core CRISPR-Cas system is composed of a cas operon flanked by two divergently organized arrays: CRISPR2 and CRISPR1. Meanwhile, the isolated CRISPR array, CRISPR3, was found ~1.3 million bp away from cas. The cas and three CRISPR arrays together function toward adaptive immunity, eliminating plasmids engineered with protospacer targets. If plasmids possessed an intact protospacer adjacent motif (PAM), hyperactive adaptation was stimulated in all CRISPR arrays of PA10145, whereas minimal to no adaptation was observed when the PAM was mutated. Spacer acquisition via interference-driven adaptation proceeds through strand-biased priming in PA10145. Interestingly, the isolated CRISPR3 and cas-adjacent CRISPR2 have nearly identical leader sequences, with only 3 bp mismatches. Of the 1,196 P. aeruginosa genomes analyzed, all 281 isolated arrays only occur as type I-F with similarly matching leaders to CRISPR2. Integrative conjugative elements and prophages only associate with CRISPR2 and CRISPR3, suggesting that isolated arrays might have originated from recombination events involving CRISPR2 as facilitated by these highly transmissible mobile genetic elements. Tracing evolutionary trajectories of the isolated CRISPR3 relative to cas-adjacent arrays revealed that CRISPR3 is horizontally transferred across P. aeruginosa genomes. Taken together, these results implicate the role of horizontally acquired isolated arrays in CRISPR-mediated pan-immunity as gateways to mobilize genetic memories. [IMPORTANCE] Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat (CRISPR) arrays are typically located adjacent to cas genes, constituting the adaptive immune system. However, a substantial subset of CRISPR arrays, called isolated arrays, is found distantly located from their cognate cas operons. Despite their prevalence, the functional significance and evolutionary implications of isolated arrays have remained poorly understood. Here, we show that isolated arrays are active components of type I-F CRISPR-Cas systems in Pseudomonas aeruginosa. These arrays are continuously updated through hyperactive strand-biased primed adaptation and are transferred horizontally across P. aeruginosa, acting as conduits of immunological memory and proponents of CRISPR-mediated pan-immunity. We posit that bacterial populations mobilize these isolated arrays to maintain transferable memory in the pangenome while remaining compatible with ongoing horizontal gene transfer.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: The lysine acetyltransferase Rv0998 coordinates transcriptional and metabolic adaptation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to acidic pH.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) survives host defenses by adapting to host conditions, including acid stress, during infection. A critical survival strategy involves pH homeostasis, mediated by complex signaling systems that regulate metabolic reprogramming and stress responses. While the lysine acetyltransferase Rv0998 is known to support Mtb hypoxia adaptation and metabolic flexibility, its role in acid stress remains unexplored. Here, we investigated the consequences of rv0998 deletion in 7H9 with glucose as the major carbon source. RNA-seq analysis showed that loss of Rv0998 altered the transcriptional response to acidic pH, including changes in the DosR regulon and pfkB/Rv2029c. Stable isotope tracing with [U-13C6]-glucose also showed reduced fractional 13C labeling across central carbon metabolites in the rv0998 mutant, with the largest decrease at acidic pH observed in upper glycolytic and connected hexose-phosphate intermediates. Growth and glucose-labeling phenotypes of dosR and pfkB mutants provided focused examples of stress-responsive and carbon-metabolic processes associated with the broader Rv0998 response. These findings indicate that Rv0998 contributes to coordinated transcriptional and metabolic adaptation of Mtb to acidic pH, and support further investigation of how stress-responsive regulatory programs are coupled to carbon metabolism during acid adaptation.IMPORTANCEMycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) persists in host environments that are both acidic and nutritionally variable, but the regulatory processes that connect these stresses to metabolism remain incompletely understood. We show that loss of the lysine acetyltransferase Rv0998 impairs growth at acidic pH when glucose is the major carbon source, and is accompanied by broad changes in gene expression and incorporation of glucose-derived carbon into central metabolites. The phenotype is not apparent when glycerol is also present, indicating that the response depends on carbon-source context. These findings identify Rv0998 as a contributor to the coordination of acid-stress adaptation and central carbon metabolism in Mtb, the bacterium that causes tuberculosis.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Loss of RafE impairs raffinose utilization and increases early pneumococcal burden in mice.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Streptococcus pneumoniae (the pneumococcus) is one of the most common bacterial causes of middle ear infections (otitis media) in children. These infections are highly prevalent but can be persistent and challenging to treat. The pneumococcus is a highly genetically diverse organism, but the precise molecular factors that drive infection of the ear are not fully understood. Bacterial metabolic capacity is known to play an important role in infection. Here, we explored the metabolic capacity of two serotype 3 isolates of S. pneumoniae obtained from the middle ear of children with otitis media. Serotype 3 is a clinically relevant serotype of concern due to its inadequate control despite its inclusion in pneumococcal conjugate vaccines. We identified one strain as unable to metabolize raffinose, and by coupling genomic and phenotypic methods, we showed that this metabolic defect was likely due to a premature stop codon in the gene encoding the raffinose-family oligosaccharide utilization system ABC transporter substrate-binding protein (rafE). Using a S. pneumoniae D39 serotype 2 strain as a model, we showed that construction of a rafE deletion or introduction of the variant gene resulted in an increase in the number of pneumococci in the ears of mice, suggesting that this may promote transit to, or survival at, this site. This work provides further evidence of variation at the raffinose utilization locus in pneumococci and an association with distinct virulence phenotypes. Together, this aids our understanding of these infections and may have implications for the design of new therapies and vaccines.IMPORTANCEStreptococcus pneumoniae is a bacterium that lives in the nose of healthy people but can cause a range of infections in the lungs, ears, brain, and blood. In this study, we explore how S. pneumoniae acquires nutrients and proliferates inside different sites of the body. We found that nutrient uptake pathways can differ between strains, and this changes how they infect different sites. The significance of our research is in understanding how these bacteria survive in different parts of the body, which is important for developing new ways of preventing or treating disease.

Nature Geoscience.title: Insensitivity of the North Pacific oxygen-deficient zone to recent ice age cycle climate changes
